Nasr Ahmed and Kazuharu Bamba investigate cyclic universe models with a negative, time-varying cosmological constant. Cyclic models imagine the universe bouncing rather than a single starting point. Their negative constant is meant as a new route to explain late-time cosmic acceleration.

They study two simplified non-singular models and show sound evolution with positive energy density is possible. With a positive or zero constant, negative energy density would dominate instead. In the first model, cosmic pressure flips sign in a quintessence-dominated universe with no violation of the null energy condition. In the second, a matter-bounce scenario crosses the phantom divide near the bounce. Scalar and quantum potentials sum to a negative value in their results.
arxiv-2512-14006:
Denis Potapov and co-authors extend the Fuglede commutativity theorem to symmetric spaces of measurable operators. The classical theorem links normal operators and their adjoints when they commute in one direction. Their setting is the full scale of symmetrically normed operator ideals and tau-measurable operator spaces.

They give a complete characterization: such a space satisfies the Fuglede theorem if and only if its commutative core has non-trivial Boyd indices. Equivalently, the space must be an interpolation space in the scale of L_p spaces for p between 1 and infinity. That criterion subsumes all previously known cases, including Lorentz and Schatten classes. The result unifies a scattered set of earlier theorems into one test.
arxiv-2512-14306:
Nikoleta Anesti, Edward Hill, and Andreas Joseph test whether a large language model can mimic household inflation attitudes in a 2025 paper. They use GPT 3.5 turbo and compare its answers with the Bank of England Inflation Attitudes Survey and official statistics.

The design exploits the model training cutoff in September 2021, before the UK inflation surge, so the model had no knowledge of it. GPT tracked survey and official projections at short horizons. It also copied key patterns by income, housing tenure, and social class, and showed a human like sensitivity to food inflation. But it lacked a consistent model of consumer price inflation. A Shapley value method helps explain which prompt parts drive its answers.
arxiv-2512-15606:
Carlos Couto and co authors analyze learning near an optimal point through a teacher student lens in a 2025 paper. When a neural network sits near its best fit, gradient descent behavior is governed by the Hessian matrix of the loss. The team characterizes that matrix's spectrum when teacher and student networks share matching weights.

For linear networks they prove the spectrum follows a convolution of scaled chi square and Marchenko Pastur distributions in large networks. Smaller Hessian eigenvalues set long time learning performance. Numerical work covers polynomial and other nonlinear networks, where Hessian rank acts as an effective parameter count. For generic smooth activations, the Hessian stays full rank empirically.
arxiv-2512-15806:
Gavin Putland derives generalized Gregory quadrature rules in a 2025 paper, dated December 17. Quadrature estimates an integral from values at evenly spaced points. Gregory style rules keep unit weights in the middle and add corrections at a few points near each end, using no extra information about the function.

One parameter, alpha, sets the distance from the range end to the first node in step units. Alpha of one half gives corrected midpoint rules, alpha zero gives Gregory's closed rules including the trapezoidal and Simpson rules, and alpha one gives open rules. Negative values even yield finite difference corrections, and different end values produce Adams Bashforth and Adams Moulton weights.
arxiv-2512-16006:
Agnieszka Wiszniewska-Matyszkiel and Maciej Wrona model an oil-like market in this 46-page economics paper, posted to arXiv in 2025. A cartel with market power shares a resource market with many small fringe firms, all drawing on linked deposits of a nonrenewable resource. A sustainable substitute caps the price, and each firm faces limits on how fast it can extract.

The authors fully pin down the Stackelberg equilibrium, where the cartel leads and the fringe follows. Alongside the usual outcome where both sides extract at once, they find surprising cases. For some starting capacities, the cartel does best by scaring the fringe off entirely, or by waiting until the fringe drains its own deposit first. A sensitivity study maps when each outcome wins.
arxiv-2512-16206:
Sachin R Pendse and eight co-authors examine AI chatbots in mental health care in a paper released on arXiv in 2025, accepted to a 2026 conference on AI ethics and society. People in distress often cannot see how a human therapist reads their words or decides on treatment. Chatbots add a second black box: users get no view of how the model processed their pain or why it answered as it did.

The authors argue that people in severe distress need a higher standard of openness than casual chatbot users. They propose reflective interpretability, designs that invite users to question and make their own meaning from model output instead of obeying it as instruction. Drawing on psychotherapy, crisis work, psychiatry, and care authorization, they suggest tools like role induction, advance directives, and clear paths to human recourse, with risks noted.
arxiv-2512-16306:
Adam Nowak, Pawel Plewa, and Tomasz Z Szarek tidy a corner of analysis in a 81-page arXiv paper posted in 2025. The Jacobi heat kernel describes how heat spreads in settings governed by Jacobi polynomials, and sharp two-sided bounds for it were assembled piecemeal across several recent papers.

The authors give one unified, optimized proof of those bounds. Their emphasis falls on tracing and estimating every constant that appears along the way, work earlier proofs left loose. That bookkeeping pays off: the multiplicative constants in the final bounds are now controlled quantitatively in terms of the parameters. The control carries over to related kernels, including the spherical heat kernel and all heat kernels on compact rank one symmetric spaces, where the associated dimension enters explicitly.
arxiv-2512-16406:
Joachim Winther Pedersen and six co-authors build self-evolving networks in a 2025 paper on arXiv. Evolution normally needs an outside optimizer to mutate and select. The team asks whether a neural network can carry that machinery inside itself.

Their Self-Referential Graph HyperNetworks generate their own parameters stochastically, mutate, and judge the results, with mutation rates themselves evolving as traits. On new benchmarks with sudden environmental shifts, versions of pole balancing and lunar landing that change mid-run, the systems adapted swiftly and reliably. On a locomotion task, they evolved coherent gaits and learned to reduce variation once good solutions appeared, concentrating the population. The authors read this as evidence that evolvability can emerge from neural self-reference, a step toward open-ended learning agents.
arxiv-2512-16506:
Chin-Yu Hsiao and Ood Shabtai study Toeplitz operators on CR manifolds, which are spaces that mix features of complex and real geometry. Their operator is built from a classical pseudo-differential operator on a compact, strictly convex CR space that can be embedded.

The main result gives a formula for the diagonal values of the second term in the symbol expansion of the operator kernel. The authors also build full step-by-step expansions for Toeplitz operators on the positive part of a compact CR orbifold, under mild extra conditions. Such formulas help link local data on the space to global spectral facts.
arxiv-2512-16606:
Samuel Lin, Ricardo A. E. Mendes, and Marco Radeschi ask what manifold submetries look like on compact normal homogeneous spaces. A submetry is a map that does not stretch distances, and singular foliations, which slice a space into leaves of mixed size, give key examples.

Their main finding is that such maps on these spaces always have an algebraic form, built from polynomial-like data. They also show a one-to-one match between submetries and algebras of algebraic functions kept fixed by the Laplace-Beltrami operator. A step along the way shows that the mean curvature field of the fibers is basic, meaning it comes from the base space.
arxiv-2512-16706:
Antonella Rech, Nicola Conci, and Nicola Garau present SDFoam, a method that rebuilds 3D surfaces from images more cleanly than past tools. Ray-traced and splat-based methods render views well, but both tend to give messy meshes with stray floaters and weak shape detail.

SDFoam learns an explicit Voronoi foam together with an implicit signed distance field, which records how far each point sits from the surface. A rule that keeps that field well behaved pushes cell faces to line up with the true surface. Across varied scenes, meshes got much sharper and more faithful, with view quality and training speed on par with RadiantFoam, the method it builds on.
arxiv-2512-17006:
Matthew Golden presents an explicit sixth-order Runge-Kutta method built for simple Lawson integration, a scheme for stiff problems where a stiff linear part is handled by matrix exponentiation. Plain explicit methods fail when stiffness is present, as in many fluid and plasma runs.

Any Runge-Kutta scheme can drive Lawson integration, but the code stays simple when step points are ordered and evenly spaced. Classic RK4 fits, yet higher-order fits were hard to find. Golden method, found with Newton-Raphson iteration, meets the spacing rule at sixth order. That gives a high-accuracy Lawson scheme that stays easy to implement.
arxiv-2512-17506:
Brienna M Larrick and many co-authors describe the HEAL Data Platform, a single search door for research on addiction and pain. The United States HEAL Initiative funds over a thousand studies, yet their data sat scattered across many separate archives. A researcher hunting one topic had to knock on every door and learn every archive's own system.

Built on the open Gen3 software, the platform links nineteen repositories and study collections behind one login and one metadata scheme. Hundreds of users a month search across all of them at once. Secure cloud workspaces then let visitors analyze data where it lives, without bulk downloads. By keeping data findable and reusable, the platform squeezes more science from studies already paid for.
arxiv-2512-17806:
Dario Dennstädt, Janina Schaa, and Thomas Berger tackle a control problem: making an unknown nonlinear system follow a chosen output path. Their systems have several inputs and outputs, relative degree two, and stable hidden dynamics. The goal is to keep the tracking error inside set limits called a funnel.

Their controller is adaptive and needs no model of the system. An output filter lets it work without measuring how fast the output changes. The design guarantees that the error stays within the funnel bounds at all times. A worked number example shows the method in action.
arxiv-2512-18006:
Alexey S. Koshelev, Oleg Melichev, and Leslaw Rachwal study a version of gravity designed to stay free of ghost particles. The theory adds endless derivative terms, shaped by special functions, which makes it workable at high energy but spread out in space. A key test is whether its worst high energy infinities cancel at the first loop.

Using a heat kernel method, the team computes those terms and finds the exact conditions for them to vanish. Some shaping functions inside a known family pass the test, and some outside it pass as well. They also give a general formula for how the theory's couplings run with energy for a broad class of shapes.
arxiv-2512-18206:
Trevor Stepp, Parthan Olikkal, Ramana Vinjamuri, and Rajasekhar Anguluri at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County study motor synergies, the shared hand joint patterns the brain reuses across tasks. Each synergy fires at a task dependent time shift. Older two stage methods first extract candidate waveforms, then pick shifted templates with sparse fitting. That route needs at least two datasets, which complicates data collection.

Their 2025 framework learns a small set of synergies and their sparse firing weights jointly, from a single dataset. Group sparsity selects which synergies survive, while element wise sparsity pins down firing timing. An alternating minimization method drives the learning. Coefficient updates separate cleanly across tasks, and pattern updates reduce to regularized least squares problems. Tests show the method reconstructs hand velocities accurately with compact, readable synergies. Halving the data burden matters for prosthetics and recovery robotics, where recording sessions are costly.
arxiv-2512-18406:
Charilaos Kapelonis leads a five author team teaching a computer to trace every tile in an ancient mosaic. Mosaics crumble with age, and a faithful digital copy starts with marking each small piece, called a tessera, apart from the grout. Doing that by hand across a whole floor is slow and costly.

They fine tuned Meta's Segment Anything Model 2 on a fresh hand marked mosaic set they built for the task. On their test images the overlap score rose from eighty-nine to ninety-one point zero two percent, and the recall from ninety-two point one two to ninety-five point eight nine percent. On an older benchmark the model beat past methods by 3 percent on the F score and cut the tile count error from zero point two zero to zero point zero two.
arxiv-2512-18506:
Yotam Svoray builds a theory of isolated singularities, the sharp points where a geometric shape fails to be smooth, in a setting where two kinds of arithmetic mix. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works over discrete valuation rings in mixed characteristic (0,p). Classical singularity theory was built over ordinary fields; moving it to these rings takes new tools.

He defines analogues of the classical Tjurina and Milnor numbers, two counts that measure how singular a point is. He also proves generalized versions of the determinacy theorem and the Mather-Yau theorem for complete Noetherian local rings. New numerical invariants give separate tests for spotting isolated singularities in the unramified and ramified cases. The results extend a core part of algebraic geometry to arithmetic settings used in number theory.
arxiv-2512-19106:
Soto Hisakawa, Shizuo Kaji, and Ryo Kawai compare what constant curvature forces on smooth surfaces versus faceted ones. For a smooth closed surface in space, constant Gaussian curvature leaves only the sphere. In the faceted world, curvature sits at vertices as an angle defect, and the rules loosen a great deal.

The authors prove that any closed surface, orientable or not and of any genus, can be built as a polyhedron in space with the same angle defect at every vertex. Self-intersection is allowed. The proof is constructive and elementary. The result shows how much weaker curvature limits are for discrete surfaces than for smooth ones.
arxiv-2512-19206:
Tao Zhang, Ziqian Zeng, Hao Peng, and Huiping Zhuang shrink the memory that long reasoning chains eat in language models. A running model stores keys and values for every token, and chain-of-thought answers make that cache huge. Squeezing it to few bits often wrecks hard reasoning.

Their method, MixKVQ, judges each key channel twice: how hard it is to quantize, and how much the current query needs it. Channels that matter keep higher precision, while values get per-token quantization. The plug-in design needs no retraining. On complex reasoning sets, it beat earlier low-bit methods by a clear margin, easing both memory and delay.
arxiv-2512-19306:
Shakir Ali, Atif Ahmad Khan, and Abhishek Kesarwani construct special error-correcting matrices over Galois rings. Cauchy MDS matrices spread data so that any square piece can rebuild the whole, a property prized in codes and ciphers. Building many of them over rings, rather than plain fields, widens the design space.

Their approach uses nilpotent elements and the Teichmüller set of the ring to cut down the entries that must be chosen. With Frobenius maps they generate a large family of distinct functions that keep the MDS property. Further results use ring symmetries to spin new matrices from old ones, giving builders a steady supply.
arxiv-2512-19406:
Ashok Joshi, Vishva Patel, and Parth Varasani ask whether a dark shadow in a telescope image proves a black hole's photon sphere exists. The Event Horizon Telescope image of our galaxy's center looks much like a Schwarzschild black hole shadow. Yet a shadow-like patch might form without the ring of unstable light orbits outside the object.

Applying Simpson-Visser smoothing to naked and charged singularity metrics, they compute the optical appearance. In a charged case, a shadow-like region forms with no exterior photon sphere at all. Elsewhere, the regular core, not a photon sphere, sets the shadow's edge. Mimicry, they conclude, is a real hazard.
arxiv-2512-19506:
Hongliang Li, Nong Zhang, Zhewen Xu, and Xiang Li build a neural forecaster for the Madden-Julian Oscillation, the great eastward pulse of tropical rain that shapes weather weeks ahead. Physics-based prediction is costly and wobbles with the seasons. Plain neural nets are cheap but have never matched the best physics runs at longer leads.

Their DK-STN starts from a spatio-temporal network and embeds expert domain knowledge inside it. The hybrid keeps neural speed and stability while closing much of the accuracy gap toward the operational European forecasts. The authors frame the gain as proof that climate structure, handed to the network directly, beats data alone.
arxiv-2512-19806:
Alberto Spalvieri, Sébastien Garmier, and Flaminia Giacomini face a clash between two fields. Quantum information work assumes the world splits into parts, with a clean product structure. Gauge theories ban just that split for fields like electromagnetism. With no parts, even basic rules, like the LOCC theorem, cannot be brought in as they stand.

The team works with a two-dimensional lattice gauge model. It keeps the key traits of electromagnetism. They build local algebras that respect the gauge rules. They also build a sound stand-in for the split into parts. In that frame they prove a twin of the LOCC theorem. Field-linked entanglement cannot show up with no real quantum field effects at work. The result bears on planned tests of whether gravity must be quantum. There, linked entanglement is the planned witness.
arxiv-2512-20006:
Sukumar Kishanthan and Asela Hevapathige redesign the activation function to fight class imbalance. When training data favor one class by far, classifiers learn to neglect the rare class. Most fixes resample the data first, or adjust the outputs last. Their activation, OGAB, steps in during training. It acts where the embeddings form. It needs no explicit label facts to do so.

Two tools do the work. Orthogonal maps keep features independent. That saves rare-class facts that majority rule would crush in the embedding space. A group-aware bias tool sniffs out natural clusters in the data. It then shifts embeddings to widen the gaps between classes on its own. On real and synthetic imbalanced data sets, OGAB beat classic and learnable rivals. The gains were steady across the tests.
arxiv-2512-20406:
M Cristina Câmara, C Carteiro, and C Diogo compare three ways of describing the same objects in hard analysis. Toeplitz kernels arise in operator theory and can be defined through Riemann-Hilbert problems, through maximal functions, or through multipliers acting on model spaces. Each definition highlights different structure.

The paper maps how the three characterizations relate. Symbol factorization turns out to be the key that produces multipliers from a model space onto a Toeplitz kernel, including isometric ones that preserve size exactly. Maximal functions, meanwhile, connect deeply to a conjugation that the kernel carries naturally. For specialists in operator theory, the unified picture clarifies which tool to reach for when a problem arrives in one disguise or another.
arxiv-2512-20606:
Soowon Son and co-authors ask which visual backbone a point tracker should borrow. Tracking points through video demands features that stay coherent over time, yet most trackers use backbones never designed for that. The authors run the first side-by-side zero-shot comparison of large visual models on standard and robustness benchmarks for point tracking.

Video diffusion transformers win consistently, beating even ResNet backbones supervised directly on tracking data. The authors credit large-scale video pre-training, full three-dimensional attention, and its training objective. Their DiTracker pipes diffusion features into existing trackers through cost matching, fusion with a light ResNet branch, and LoRA fine-tuning. Trained only on synthetic data, it beats a leading tracker trained with real videos, above all under damage.
arxiv-2512-20806:
Anselm Paulus and six co-authors turn chatbot safety training into a game between two models. Usually, defenders train against attack prompts gathered in advance, so training proceeds in separate rounds. Here an Attacker model invents prompts while a Defender model learns to answer safely, both improving together through online reinforcement learning.

Rewards come from pairwise preferences rather than single scores, which the authors say curbs reward hacking. Their recipe, AdvGame, produced a defender that was both more helpful and harder to attack. The attacker, meanwhile, grew into a general red-teaming tool able to probe other models. The contest format keeps pressure on both sides throughout training.
arxiv-2512-21106:
Safal Thapaliya, Chuxu Zhang, and four co-authors argue that graph learning's generalization problem lives in the data, not the model. In some graphs the predictive signal sits in what nodes say; in others, in how they connect. No fixed model bias wins both games, and endlessly patching architectures cannot cover open-ended real-world diversity. Their data-centric alternative treats each node's description as adjustable: a graph network first scores predictive states, and nodes similar in structure and meaning are retrieved from the same graph as exemplars.

Those exemplars guide a language model in rewriting node descriptions for the task at hand, a step earlier language-model approaches skipped by generating text without graph context. Gains appear consistently on both text-rich and text-free graphs, and on semantics-led and structure-led problems alike. Fix the descriptions, the results suggest, and ordinary models travel further.
arxiv-2512-21406:
D. G. Nanopoulos, P. Laskos-Patkos, and Ch. C. Moustakidis examine the compact star inside the supernova remnant HESS J1731-347. Recent analyses gave it a surprisingly low mass, about three quarters of the Sun's mass, and a radius near ten kilometers. Its surface is also hot for its estimated age of a few thousand years.

The authors test three possible natures for the star: ordinary hadronic matter, a hybrid with a quark core, and a full strange star. They compute cooling curves, which track how fast the star loses heat through neutrinos, and compare them with the measured temperature and age. Hadronic models fit the data whether or not pairing effects are included. Hybrid and strange stars can also fit, but only if the quark matter is superconducting and the fastest neutrino process stays blocked. The results narrow down what this unusually light compact star could be made of.
arxiv-2512-21606:
Jiaqun Jiang introduces the shell formula, for writing down partition functions whose pole structure is built from Young diagrams of any dimension. Such functions sit at the heart of supersymmetric gauge theory and enumerative geometry, where they count instantons, localized field setups that dominate many quantum corrections.

The formalism gives explicit closed-form expressions for many systems. Its uses include the instanton partition functions of five-dimensional pure super Yang-Mills theory with classical gauge groups. It also covers gauge origami setups named the magnificent four, and spiked instantons. Donaldson-Thomas invariants in three and four dimensions fall under the same umbrella. One shell formula replacing many case-by-case computations is the selling point: the Young-diagram counting is done once and then specialized.
arxiv-2512-21706:
Shuchang Pan, Gopala Anumanchipalli, Jiachen Lian, and their co-authors teach machines to reason about conversational behavior in full-duplex speech, where both sides can talk and listen at once. Human conversation runs on an implicit chain of intentions that surfaces as timed speech acts: interruptions, backchannels, turn-taking. Interactive systems need to foresee those acts, not merely transcribe words.

The method treats the intent-to-action pathway as causal inference inside a graph of thoughts. A labeling scheme predicts high-level intents and low-level speech acts together, learning their causal and temporal links. Training data mixes event-rich simulations with human-annotated rationales and recorded conversations. During a live dialogue, the system keeps an evolving graph of its streaming predictions. A multimodal transformer forecasts the next speech act, gives a reason, and revises its reasoning as talk unfolds. Tests show robust behavior detection and readable reasoning chains.
arxiv-2512-21806:
Douglas P. Wiens works on experimental design when the model being fitted may be wrong. In robust design, a strategy is minimax: choose the design minimizing the worst prediction error over a class of models. That worst-case error splits into a variance part and a bias part caused by the model errors.

Wiens studies two constrained versions of the problem. One minimizes the predictors' variance subject to a cap on the worst-case bias. The other minimizes the worst-case bias subject to a cap on the variance. He shows the solutions to both are the minimax designs, with their tuning constants chosen appropriately. Conversely, every minimax design solves each constrained problem for a suitable cap. The result ties three design philosophies: tuning a minimax design is the same act as choosing how much bias or variance to tolerate. One family of designs serves all three purposes.
arxiv-2512-21906:
Reaction-diffusion waves of FKPP type usually spread both ways, but a random drift with positive average can hijack the fronts. Dihang Guan, Hui He, Wenqing Hu, and Jiaojiao Yang study wave propagation under random drift. They prove both the rightward and leftward fronts get pushed negative, so both may travel toward negative infinity.

The proof runs through the large deviations principle for diffusions in random environments and a Feynman-Kac analysis. Physically, the drift acts as an external field shifting the quenched free-energy reference level while leaving the system's intrinsic fluctuation structure untouched. The result clarifies how environmental flow fields redirect invasion fronts in heterogeneous media.
arxiv-2512-22106:
Zubair Shah and Noaman Khan reframe neural network pruning, the trimming of unneeded model parts, as a game. Instead of scoring parts by importance or forcing sparsity with penalties, they treat groups of weights, neurons, or filters as players. Each player chooses how much to take part in the network, weighing its contribution against redundancy and competition from others.

In this setup, sparsity appears on its own: when joining in becomes a losing strategy, a player's participation collapses to zero. The authors show this collapse happens under mild conditions and turn the idea into a simple pruning algorithm that updates weights and participation together. Tests on standard benchmarks give sparsity and accuracy trade-offs competitive with established pruning methods.
arxiv-2512-22206:
Yogeswar Reddy Thota introduces CosineGate, a method that lets residual networks skip work they do not need. Deep residual networks normally run every block on every input, even when simply passing the input through would do. CosineGate instead watches how the block's output compares with its input, using a cosine incompatibility ratio as a self-supervised signal for when a block adds nothing.

A Gumbel-Softmax relaxation makes the per-sample, per-block skip decisions trainable end to end, and a progressive penalty on total computation keeps usage in check. On CIFAR-10, settings span a frontier from aggressive savings to conservative ones. A balanced setup reached 91.3 percent accuracy while cutting computation by 28.5 percent, matching a full ResNet-20 at lower cost and without extra supervision or distillation.
arxiv-2512-22606:
Hesam Taghipour, Alireza Rezaee, and Farshid Hajati forecast gold prices by chaining memory networks into a perceptron. Gold's price tangles with macroeconomic, energy, stock, and currency forces, making accurate prediction notoriously hard. Two long short-term memory networks forecast on daily and monthly horizons respectively. They predict the next day's high, low, and closing prices. Their outputs feed a multilayer perceptron that issues the final forecast.

Network sizes were tuned by the Gray Wolf Optimizer, hunting the neuron counts with the least error. Training data ran from 2010 to 2021 across economic indicators and markets of developed countries. The authors report very small errors on daily closing prices and describe a live-trading strategy built on the forecasts that returned 171 percent over three months in their account.
arxiv-2512-22706:
Paul Dobre, Jackson Cooper, Xin Wang, and Hongzhou Yang present SCPainter, a system that inserts computer-generated cars into street scenes and then renders the result from new viewpoints. Autonomous driving simulators need diverse training data, including rare long-tail situations, which means realistic asset insertion and novel view synthesis should work together rather than in separate tools. Current insertion methods botch lighting and shadows, while view synthesis ignores inserted actors.

SCPainter represents cars as 3D Gaussian splats and the scene as a point cloud. It projects both into the requested novel view. A diffusion model, conditioned on those projections, then paints the final image. Evaluations on the Waymo Open Dataset show the combined pipeline producing diverse, realistic driving scenes for training.
arxiv-2512-22806:
Jorge Poveda and Mahmoud Abdelgalil develop stability tests for a broad family of messy dynamic systems: ones that mix fast and slow continuous motion with sudden discrete jumps, all under random disturbances. Such systems are hard to certify directly, because the behavior couples differential inclusions for the flow with difference inclusions for the jumps.

The authors build composite Foster functions, energy-like certificates assembled from simpler functions belonging to the slow and fast subsystems separately. Under standard regularity and causality assumptions on solutions, these composite functions certify stability toward compact sets and recurrence toward bounded open sets. Worked examples include switching systems whose modes change randomly on their own, feedback optimization running on randomly switching plants, and momentum-based tuning with random restarts. The point is modularity: prove simple pieces once, then combine them into a guarantee for the whole system.
arxiv-2512-23306:
Yu Jia and co-authors predict a new signal in collisions where two heavy ions miss each other. In ultraperipheral collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, the ions' photon clouds collide instead. Those photons are linearly polarized. The property matters for lepton and light hadron production, but was never checked for heavy quarkonium. The channels studied produce a J/psi meson together with a photon or a second J/psi.

Combining nonrelativistic QCD factorization with transverse-momentum-dependent photon distributions, the authors compute the lowest-order helicity amplitudes. Interference between the polarized photon states yields azimuthal asymmetries, periodic patterns in the production angle with twofold and fourfold rhythms. These ratios of weighted to unweighted cross sections should survive higher-order corrections and errors in the nonperturbative inputs, the authors argue. That makes the asymmetries a test of how quarkonium is produced and of the photon's structure at extreme energies.
arxiv-2512-23406:
Ayushman Raghuvanshi, Gonzalo Mateos, and Sundeep Prabhakar Chepuri teach graph neural networks to handle heterophilic graphs, networks where linked nodes usually carry different labels. Friendship-style homophily is the easy case; in heterophilic data, feature similarity gives weak clues about which edges matter, and standard networks blur the very differences that carry the signal. Their framework, FgGSL, learns the graph structure itself, guided by frequency information.

A learnable masking function infers two complementary graphs from node features, one homophilic and one heterophilic, and a spectral encoder processes them through pre-designed low-pass and high-pass filter banks. A label-based structural loss pushes the learned graphs to recover the right edge types, making the structure learning explicitly task-driven. The authors derive stability bounds for that loss and robustness guarantees for the filters under graph perturbations. On six heterophilic benchmarks, FgGSL consistently beat leading graph networks and rewiring methods.
arxiv-2512-23606:
Z. M. McIntyre, Ji Zou, Jelena Klinovaja, and Daniel Loss show how a magnet can become an ultra-precise sensor. Their field is quantum magnonics: magnons are quantized waves of spin in a magnet, and in anisotropic ferromagnets the ground state naturally squeezes these magnons, a genuinely quantum form of correlations. The team couples such a magnet to a single qubit.

Their protocol suddenly changes, or quenches, the ferromagnet while watching only the qubit. When ground-state squeezing is present, measurements of the qubit reveal the frequency of the coupled magnon-qubit system with Heisenberg-limited precision, the best scaling quantum mechanics allows. Without squeezing, the same measurement learns nothing. The scheme is distinctive because it uses equilibrium squeezing, a resource magnetic systems provide for free.
arxiv-2512-23806:
Jacob Bourjaily, Michael Plesser, and Cristian Vergu organize the color bookkeeping of particle physics. When particles carrying color charge scatter, every amplitude splits into kinematic pieces and color tensors built from the gauge group's algebra. Choosing a good basis of those tensors is essential for computation, and existing choices, such as multi-traces, come with redundancies and complications.

The authors construct, from any single trivalent tree graph, a spanning set of color tensors that are independent and mutually orthogonal by construction, sufficient to all orders of perturbation theory and beyond. Clebsch-Gordan coefficients at the graph's vertices connect the external particles' representations to internal irreducible ones. Any Feynman diagram's color factor then decomposes into this basis in a fixed order. At eighty pages with many tables and figures, the paper serves as a reference for amplitude users comparing bases. It is a reference work, built to be consulted.
arxiv-2512-24706:
Sheng-Qi Zhang and Cong-Feng Qiao review baryons and baryoniums through QCD sum rules, a method that links quark-level theory to hadron properties. Interest in six-quark states grew after tetraquark and pentaquark confirmations, and BESIII observations of states near eighteen forty megaelectronvolts support predicted proton-antiproton bound states. Such baryon-antibaryon systems, called baryoniums, are promising hexaquark candidates.

Investigations of baryoniums and their constituent baryons are surveyed comprehensively within the sum rule approach. Hadron physics readers get an organized account of masses and related predictions. The review helps judge which claimed exotic states the theory genuinely supports.
arxiv-2601-07106:
Jeremy Mould and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers more power on large scales. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The high value of the cosmic microwave dipole may be telling us that dark matter is macroscopic rather than a fundamental particle.

The possible presence of a significant dark matter component in. The form of primordial black holes (PBHs) sug gests that dark halo formation simulations should be commenced well before redshift z = 100. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07206:
Research by Hao Li and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with LLMRouterBench. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Large language model (LLM) routing assigns each query to the most suitable model from an ensemble. The authors introduce LLMRouterBench, a large-scale benchmark and unified framework for LLM routing.

It comprises over 400K instances from 21 datasets and 33 models. Moreover, it provides comprehensive metrics for both performance-oriented and performance-cost trade-off routing, and integrates 10 representative routing baselines. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07306: Nesar Ramachandra and co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how the cosmos builds its large shapes. Gravity rules that build at the grand scale. Gas and stars add a push at scales near one megaparsec. To catch that push, a model must track gas flow and star-based steps. Those steps are too fine to run in full, so models pack them into short-cut rules called subgrid models. The authors use a fast stand-in, called an emulator, to test many subgrid picks at low cost.
arxiv-2601-07506:
Dongryeol Lee and colleagues probe a weak spot in using language models as graders. Many teams now let an LLM judge answers to questions against a given reference. Lee's team asks whether judges actually follow that reference. Their 2026 preprint reports a critical failure mode in reference-based evaluation.

When the reference conflicts with what the judge model already believes, scores turn unreliable. The model leans on its own stored knowledge instead of the text it was given. That drift substantially lowers evaluation fidelity, the authors report. The finding matters wherever LLM judges score question answering at scale. It warns builders to test judges against references that deliberately contradict common knowledge.
arxiv-2601-07606:
Bingyang Ye and colleagues ask how anyone can grade a model's judgment of new research ideas. Large language models now assess and forecast scientific ideas, yet checking those judgments is hard. Their 2026 preprint introduces Proof of Time, a benchmarking framework that is semi-verifiable. It ties judgments made today to signals that only become visible later.

An idea judged promising can later be tested by what actually happens in science. That delay is the point: time itself supplies the ground truth. The framework aims to scale, so many judgments can be scored without endless expert review. Better benchmarks for idea judgment matter as labs use models to pick research directions. The paper speaks to AI evaluators and science funders alike.
arxiv-2601-07706:
Andy Haverly, Shahram Rahimi, and Mark A. Novotny map classical computer instructions into a quantum computing form. Their 2026 preprint transforms ARM assembly instructions for use in quantum algorithms. ARM assembly is a staple low-level language in classical computing. The core achievement is a direct mapping from that language to quantum paradigms. The team shows the method by computing the Fibonacci sequence.

A worked example matters because it proves the mapping can run a real algorithm. Bridging classical assembly and quantum circuits could lower the entry barrier for programmers. It also raises questions about which classical patterns translate usefully. The paper speaks to quantum software scholars exploring new compilation paths. It treats assembly as a possible front end for quantum programs, not just a hardware detail.
arxiv-2601-08106:
Sergio Cabello, Timothy Chan, and Panos Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations with help from predictions. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a basic task in computational geometry. Given points in the plane, the Delaunay triangulation is a standard mesh with strong shape properties.

The setting adds a predicted triangulation G, a guess at the correct answer. When G lies close to the true triangulation, an algorithm should finish faster than starting cold. The authors ask how to use a good guess without being hurt by a bad one. Their work joins a growing line on algorithms that learn from predictions while keeping firm guarantees.
arxiv-2601-08206:
Vedad Dzanic and three co-authors review lattice Boltzmann methods for non-Newtonian fluids. Their 2026 arXiv review appeared in the Journal of Non-Newtonian Fluid Mechanics. Such fluids break the single constant viscosity rule that simple flow models assume.

Common traits include shear-thinning, shear-thickening, viscoplasticity, and viscoelasticity. Everyday examples range over ketchup, blood, toothpaste, and mud. Lattice Boltzmann methods simulate flow on a grid of particle distributions, which suits complex behavior. The review gathers how these methods handle each non-Newtonian trait. Engineers and researchers get one reference for simulating fluids that refuse to act like water.
arxiv-2601-08806:
Abhi Kottamasu and seven co-authors set up a test of AI on real paid code work. Many tests ask a model to fix a small bug in a toy task. Paid work is broader. It can mean new features, long files, and talks with a client brief. The team wants a test that fits that real scope.

Their test is called APEX-SWE. It grades top models on tasks with real cash value in code work. Each task asks for a full piece of work, not a lone code line. Scores show if a model can do work a firm would pay for. A reader who hires or builds code AI gets a hard, fair scale for that claim.
arxiv-2601-09206:
Song-lin Zhao, Xiao-gang Mu, and Da-jun Zhang turn a smooth model into a step form that a PC can run. The model is the Mikhailov model, a pair of linked wave rules. A step form swaps smooth change for hops on a grid. Done with care, the step form keeps the deep traits of the smooth one, such as its set of saved counts.

They use a matrix sum path to build the step form. They also build a pair of step Miura maps, which tie the model to a known wave chain. One rule of the pair comes from how those maps fit. A reader in wave math gets a step twin for a classic model.
arxiv-2601-09306:
Xin Xia, Hongzhi Yin, and Shane Culpepper bring large chat models to pick work that runs on the phone itself. On phone picks have clear gains. They are fast, they keep user data on the phone, and they work with no net. But chat models are vast. Their RAM and power needs can swamp a phone, so a plain port is a high risk bet.

The team gives ways to shrink and speed such models for step by step picks. Each pick rests on the user's past picks in a row. The model has to scan that row and call the next item, all on the phone. A reader in phone AI gets a path to private, fast picks with no host in the loop.
arxiv-2601-09606:
Manning Gao and five co-authors rethink how machines judge the mood of a clip. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents GRCF, a two-stage framework for multimodal sentiment analysis. Most past work used pointwise regression, predicting one score per clip.

A single score is fragile under label noise and ignores whether one clip is more positive than another. Pairwise methods learn from comparisons instead. GRCF adds group-wise ranking with a calibration stage. Judging relative order first, then calibrating the scores, should steady predictions across text, audio, and video used together. It also makes the final scores easier to compare across datasets.
arxiv-2601-09706:
Andreea Dutulescu, Stefan Ruseti, and Mihai Dascalu target a blind spot of transformer language models: numbers. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes value-aware representations for numbers. Models often ace hard math benchmarks yet slip on basic arithmetic.

The root cause, the authors argue, is that numbers enter as symbols. Their embeddings do not state the value the number stands for. That gap produces systematic errors in simple tasks. Teaching the representation to carry value could firm up everyday calculation. It is a small, targeted fix aimed at a surprisingly common and costly failure.
arxiv-2601-10406:
Weiping Fu and co authors grade quiz items by their flaws, not by one score. Auto quiz makers can write items with deep flaws. A fact may be false. The marked answer may not fit the ask. Past grade tools give one whole score. That can hide a flaw and rate a bad item high.

The team built ErrEval, a grade tool that names flaws. It lists each flaw it finds in plain tags. The score then rests on those tags. Labs can see why an item lost marks. The work aims for grades that match how a human pro would fault an item.
arxiv-2601-10606:
Peng Chen, Xiaobao Wei, Yi Yang, Naiming Yao, Hui Chen, and Feng Tian build RSATalker, a system that animates talking heads for conversation. Such avatars matter more as virtual reality grows, above all in social scenes with turns of talk. Older methods split into two camps. Mesh-based 3D methods handle two-person dialogue but look fake.

Large 2D models look natural yet cost too much compute to run smoothly. RSATalker aims for realistic, socially aware faces across multi-turn exchanges. A good avatar must react to a partner, not just recite lines. The work speaks to teams building virtual meeting and social spaces where faces carry the interaction.
arxiv-2601-10706:
Quinten De Man, Atharva Sharma, Kishen N Gowda, and Laxman Dhulipala present UFO Trees, a data structure for dynamic forests. The dynamic trees problem asks software to keep a tree current as edges come and go. Queries ask whether two nodes are linked, or what lies on a path. The classic link-cut tree has led this field for forty years.

The authors' tests show link-cut trees are still the fastest sequential option. UFO Trees target parallel batch updates instead, where many changes land at once. The design claims both practical speed and proven efficiency bounds. Such structures sit inside graph analytics and network tools that must track changing connections at scale.
arxiv-2601-10906:
Mark Van Raamsdonk and Alejandro Vilar López build a menagerie of exact solutions in three-dimensional gravity. The solutions carry heavy matter particles. They generalize a construction by Antonini, Sasieta, and Swingle, known as AS2. That construction was argued to define states in a conformal field theory that are dual to a spacetime holding a closed baby universe.

A baby universe is a small cosmos pinched off from the main one. Having many exact examples lets theorists test claims about how such states behave. Holography, the duality between gravity and field theory, is the frame. The zoo of solutions gives the community concrete cases for debates about entropy and the interior of black holes.
arxiv-2601-11306:
Dimitry Gurevich studies quantum matrices of GL type in this 2026 preprint. The work sits in reflection equation algebras, a quantum algebra field. Such algebras are tied to even skew-invertible Hecke symmetries. A generating matrix, called L, holds the algebra's core data.

The main result computes characters of the spectral values of L. Those values live in finite-dimensional representations of the algebra. Each representation is labeled by a partition of an integer. Characters sum the weights of a representation in one number. Knowing them maps how the quantum matrix acts across cases. That map helps classify the representations of these algebras. The work is pure algebra with roots in quantum physics.
arxiv-2601-11506:
R. Vukelich and seven coauthors build a terahertz spectrometer for deep cold. Their 2026 preprint puts the system in a dilution refrigerator. Terahertz time-domain spectroscopy probes quantum materials with light. A dilution refrigerator reaches temperatures far below 1 K.

The fridge is a Bluefors unit with a 7 T split-coil magnet. The team measured waveforms at 145 mK in the setup. Fields ran from 0 to 6 Tesla during the runs. The test sample was a gallium arsenide quantum well. Cyclotron resonance was the target signal in the well. Cold, high-field terahertz tools open new states to study. Quantum materials often hide their traits at just such extremes.
arxiv-2601-11606:
Farzana Islam Adiba and five coauthors build a pipeline for the MIMIC-IV dataset. Their 2026 preprint handles the resource's many data kinds at once. MIMIC-IV is a large public electronic health record set. Clinical machine learning research uses it widely today.

The set holds structured data and clinical notes together. Waveforms and imaging data add two more kinds. These modalities sit disjointed in the raw release. Preprocessing and aligning them takes heavy manual effort. The team's pipeline automates that join across modalities. Aligned data can then feed downstream clinical studies. A shared pipeline saves each lab from redoing the grind.
arxiv-2601-12006: Rami Luisto asks if the shape of a road network can show how rural a place is. The work starts from a personal watch on Finnish roads and their shapes. City grids and country lanes form quite unlike graph shapes. He treats this as a qualitative study, not a strict count. Figures match road shapes from city and country sites with shapes from group theory. The aim is to see what geometry alone can tell.
arxiv-2601-12106:
Rodrigo Moreira, Larissa Ferreira Rodrigues Moreira, Tereza C. Carvalho, and Flávio de Oliveira Silva study noisy neighbours in beyond-5G networks. Virtual tools make mobile nets more modular and easy to scale. They also cut running costs and allow sliced nets for new uses.

In the data plane, one tenant's load can harm a neighbour's service. The team study that spill in 5G-style setups. Knowing its size helps operators set fair shares. The work links slice design to real service quality.  The study names where slice shares need firm caps.
arxiv-2601-12206:
Keng Hao Ooi sorts Sobolev multiplier spaces of Lorentz type and their preduals. Multiplier spaces hold functions that can multiply a Sobolev space into itself, or into a set target. Lorentz forms refine the scale by a second index.

He gives block forms and the Köthe dual of the preduals. As a use case, he shows the local Hardy-Littlewood maximal function is bounded on these spaces. Such bounds are core tools in harmonic analysis. The work gives a full map of this space family.  The dual work rounds out the full space map.
arxiv-2601-12406:
Keshab Chandra Bakshi studies a setup from operator algebra, where one algebra sits inside a larger one. The pair are simple unital C star algebras, and the step from small to large has finite index. Bakshi builds a canonical map on a key corner of this setup. That corner is the second relative commutant, a set of elements tied to both algebras.

The map he builds is completely positive and acts like a coproduct. With it, the corner gains the structure of a coalgebra. He calls objects of this kind weak quantum hypergroups. Such structures extend the math of symmetry past groups and quantum groups. The work gives a firm source for them from a plain inclusion of algebras.
arxiv-2601-12806:
Chih-Ting Lu and four co authors test whether a new particle could explain an excess seen at the CMS detector. The excess appears in top quark pair production data. Their candidate is a pseudoscalar particle with a mass of 365 GeV. It would live in a two Higgs doublet model, which adds a second Higgs field to the standard model.

They analyze four types of such models, labeled I, II, X, and Y. They use best fit parameters for the pseudoscalar, including its width and a key ratio called tan beta. The question is whether any conventional version of the model fits the excess. Their work was prepared for a nuclear physics journal. Such tests decide whether an anomaly needs new physics or fades away.
arxiv-2601-13106:
Vincenzo Lipardi, David Mestel, and Georgios Stamoulis study fast rough answers for a quantum magnet model. The model is the transverse field Ising model. It pairs pull or push links between qubits with a sideways field on each qubit. All weights are zero or plus.

Exact answers are hard, so the team builds classic rules that run in polynomial time. Such rules promise answers within a known gap of the best. Links may pull one way for some pairs and push for others. That mix makes the task hard yet rich. Good rough rules here help both maths and quantum staff judge what quantum tools must beat.
arxiv-2601-13206:
Neil Sehgal, Sharath Chandra Guntuku, and Lyle Ungar test if language models feel the clock in live talks. Such models write one token at a time, in set steps. Real talks, from care chats to trade deals, hinge on smooth time and hard stops. Yet most tests of such models skip time sense.

The team pairs agents in fake trade deals under strict time caps. They watch how the models shift tone and terms as the cap nears. Their finds point to flaws in time sense. A model may hold out too long or fold too late. For teams that put chat agents in live talks, the gaps flag a risk that plain text scores miss.
arxiv-2601-13906:
Andrzej Dudek and co-authors study uniform patterns in random ordered matchings in 2026. An ordered r-uniform matching is a set of disjoint r-element subsets of an ordered set. For the case of two edges, the pattern shows how the two sets intertwine. There are many such patterns, counted by a binomial formula.

The team looks for homogeneous substructures inside random matchings. Homogeneous means the small patterns inside all share one form. Random structures often hide such order at a large scale. Finding it helps combinatorics map the border of chaos and order.
arxiv-2601-14406:
Yixiong Chen, Zongwei Zhou, Wenxuan Li, and Alan Yuille tackle label quality in medical imaging in this 2026 paper. Large segmentation datasets mix manual labels with pseudo-labels of uneven quality. Bad labels can compromise both training and evaluation. They also make model training less robust.

The team built SegAE, a Segmentation Assessment Engine. It is a lightweight vision-language model that predicts label quality on its own. It covers 142 anatomical structures. Their method also uses synthetic data to teach the judge. Readers get a tool for checking label quality at a scale no human team could grade by hand.
arxiv-2601-14506:
Amogh Gupta, Niharika Patil, Sourojit Ghosh, and Snehalkumar Gaikwad study bias in AI tutoring in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM FAccT conference. AI chatbots are now popular worldwide, and students use them for coursework support. That spread creates a need to study their benefits and drawbacks. The authors ask one pointed question.

How do large language models perceive the intellectual capabilities of student profiles from intersecting marginalized identities, across distinct cultural contexts? The paper's title names its axes: language, caste, and context. It compares AI-generated explanations across Indian and American STEM educational systems. Readers get evidence on how demographic cues can shift the help students receive.
arxiv-2601-14706:
Chao Gao and a team at Gensmo.ai present a fashion search benchmark in this 2026 paper. LookBench is a live and holistic open benchmark for fashion image retrieval in real e-commerce settings. The authors use the word look in a shopper's sense. A look can mean finding the exact item, a close substitute, or a visually consistent alternative.

Most benchmarks test retrieval on clean catalog photos. Real shoppers search messy, real-world images. LookBench is built to mirror how people actually shop. It is live, so its data can refresh, and holistic, so it covers many search styles. Readers get a harder, more honest test for fashion retrieval systems.
arxiv-2601-14906:
Jan Dreier, Jakub Gajarský, and Michał Pilipczuk study ways to change a graph with logic. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with transductions, edits to a graph that first-order logic can state. The team asks how to undo such an edit, at least in rough form.

Running a transduction backwards is the hard part. The authors give a fast method that works when the source graph is sparse. Sparse here means the graph class has a bounded form of spread. The method gives an approximate reversal of the edit, not an exact one.
arxiv-2601-15106:
Giulio Bordieri, Giorgio Cartechini, and co-authors link radiation physics to cell survival with deep learning. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with proton and carbon ion beams used in therapy. How the beam's energy lands across scales helps decide the damage cells take.

Yet the link between those scales and the biological outcome is still not fully understood. The authors build a multi-scale deep learning model to predict cell survival. The model is made to stay interpretable, so its steps can be read. Their slogan is one scale to rule them all.
arxiv-2601-15406:
Hatef Otroshi Shahreza, Anjith George, and Sébastien Marcel test whether big multimodal models can match faces across sensors. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with heterogeneous face recognition. Enrollment and probe images come from different sensing modes, which makes matching hard.

The modes include visible light, near infrared, short-wave infrared, and thermal cameras. Multimodal large language models shine on many vision-language tasks. That raises hopes for biometric use. The authors run a systematic evaluation of the top models on this cross-sensor task, to see how far those high hopes truly hold up.
arxiv-2601-15606:
Jonghyeon Ahn studies barcode entropy in symplectic geometry in a 2026 arXiv paper. Barcodes come from persistence modules, which track features across scales. Barcode entropy measures how fast the count of long bars grows. Long bars signal lasting structure. Ahn's setting is the relative symplectic cohomology of a Liouville domain. That domain sits inside a larger symplectic manifold.

Symplectic cohomology is a tool for probing such spaces and their dynamics. Tying its barcodes to an entropy gives a new invariant to compute. Growth rates often reveal rigidity: some systems cannot grow past a bound. Results like this link algebra to the motion of Hamiltonian systems. The paper is aimed at specialists in symplectic topology. Its terms are technical, and the abstract states the setup with little gloss.
arxiv-2601-16306:
Emily Townsend, Joshua Pomeroy and Garnett Bryant draw a new Lindblad form for a driven spin dot. Their 2026 preprint deals with a quantum dot tied to a lead. The lead acts in a Markov way, with no long past. A wave field drives the spin state of the dot. Past Lindblad forms miss terms that the drive plus tie create.

The team draws the full form for that joint case. They show it keeps all states sound and sums to one. They also find the jump steps that the form holds. A sound form lets teams model driven dots with trust. Such dots sit at the heart of spin based quantum gear.
arxiv-2601-16606:
Antonio Bracale and three coauthors weigh flaws in base tone reads when volts waver. Their 2026 preprint deals with power grade on new grids. Base tone, the mains wave rate, is a key grade mark. True reads of it in short spans guide grid checks. New grids waver in volts far more than old grids did.

Waver bends tone reads in ways teams must count. The team tests read ways side by side in such terms. Each way is scored by its flaw size in short spans. Low flaw ways help grid teams spot faults fast. The work serves checks of grid health in real time.
arxiv-2601-16906:
Calarina Muslimani and a team of five co-authors help set reward scores for learning bots. A bot learns well when its score matches the true aim. Hand-set scores are slow to tune and oft off mark. Their 2026 preprint builds a score gauge called TAC. It rates how well a score path tracks the aim path.

The gauge first aids hand tuning of score weights. It shows which weights pull the bot off aim. Then it goes past tuning, to learn scores from data. Sound scores cut wasted runs in bot training. They also curb bots that game a poor score for gain.
arxiv-2601-17206:
Lars Andersson and Bernardo Araneda prove a result about Hermitian gravitational instantons. These are special curved spaces used in gravity theory. The authors look at the moduli space, the space of all such shapes. They show it is rigid at the small-change level. They also show small changes can be built up into full shapes.

Their result joins a recent proof by Biquard, Gauduchon, and LeBrun. That proof gave local rigidity for Hermitian instantons. Together, the two works complete the picture. The result holds for compact spaces and for open ones too. For geometers, it closes a clear gap. It tells them these rare spaces have no hidden flex.
arxiv-2601-17506:
Shohini Bhattacharya and four co-authors propose how to spot gluon GTMDs at the future Electron-Ion Collider. GTMDs are generalized transverse momentum distributions. They give a rich picture of gluons inside the proton. The team uses exclusive heavy vector meson production. Axial-vector mesons join the study too. The setting is lepton-proton collisions.

They work within collinear twist-3 factorization. In that frame, set azimuthal angle patterns mark GTMD presence. Clear signatures tell EIC teams what to measure. Gluon structure is a core EIC goal. A planned signature saves beam time and sharpens design. The work turns abstract distributions into detector targets.
arxiv-2601-18106:
Jiatan Huang and co-authors build a benchmark that joins food knowledge with health goals. Their 2026 preprint presents GLEN-Bench, a graph-language benchmark for nutritional health. Diet interventions are a main tool for managing chronic disease. Judging them needs both food facts and a patient's state. A graph can hold the links between foods, nutrients, and conditions, while language models supply the reasoning over that graph.

The benchmark tests how well systems handle such joined tasks. Nutrition advice is an area where wrong answers carry health costs. A shared test set helps compare tools on equal ground. It also shows where models still fail at diet reasoning. The work serves builders of health assistants.
arxiv-2601-18306:
Everlyn Asiko Chimoto, Mostafa Elhoushi, and Bruce Bassett argue that calibration data for shrinking models should span many languages. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantization, which cuts a model's storage and compute costs. Quantization often costs accuracy. The standard post-training methods calibrate on small English-only sets. What that choice does to multilingual models has been little studied. The authors test language diversity in calibration for quantized multilingual models.

If diverse calibration guards non-English skill, the fix is cheap and broad. Most users of these models do not work in English alone. The study gives deployment teams a concrete lever to test. It also warns against English-only habits in model tooling.
arxiv-2601-18506:
Valentin Magro, Sébastien Garcia, and Alexei Ourjoumtsev study groups of atoms that act as one big atom when raised to high states. Such a group can hold a quantum bit and can give off lone bits of light. Those skills make groups of this kind strong picks for nodes in quantum nets. To grade a group, staff need a maths that is true to life yet cheap to run.

Real groups are large and messy, with atoms spread at chance. A cheap maths that skips the mess can give the wrong grade. The team build a maths that keeps the key facts of the mess while it stays cheap to run. It deals with a flaw in which the group fails to block a next rise as well as hoped. Firm grades help labs build nodes that link well in a net.
arxiv-2601-18606:
Yanhong Lai, Xianyu Tan, and Yubo Su study the winds of small far worlds that sit tipped far on their sides. With a new space scope in use, staff can now read the air of low-mass worlds, not just of big ones. In tight groups of worlds, pulls from mates can lock a world in a tipped pose for good. A tipped world also tends to spin out of step with its path.

That pose should drive odd winds. One side may bake while the next side freezes, in a beat set by the slow spin. The team model how air moves in that case. Their maps may help staff read the light of such worlds when the scope catches them. A good wind map is key to tell a world's heat tale from a few dots of light.
arxiv-2601-18706:
Health-SCORE sets out to make the grade sheets for health chat tools cheap to build and safe to trust. A grade sheet lists the traits a good reply must show, trait by trait. Such sheets are key for open asks, where no one right reply exists. In health work they count most of all, since a bad reply can harm. But good sheets take skill and time to build by hand.

The new frame builds sheets in a way that can scale to many health fields. It cuts the hand cost while it holds the worth of the grades. Trained and graded on such sheets, health tools could get both safer and more apt. The frame aims to make that loop cheap to run for each new use. That could lift the bar for health chat as a whole.
arxiv-2601-19206:
Min Namkung and five co-authors set privacy rules for quantum sensing spread across many clients. In such networks, clients share quantum resources to measure fields at many places, while servers they may not trust help run the work. Privacy is a basic need in that setup.

Past privacy rules leaned on ideal bounds that real measurements cannot reach. The team defines privacy in operational terms, tied to what real devices can do. Workable rules let engineers promise clients a level of privacy that a lab test could check, not just a theorem could state.
arxiv-2601-19306:
Sijia Li and five co-authors give phone agents a drive to go learn what they do not know. Mobile agents can run smartphone tasks, but in complex apps they stall on missing knowledge and new screens. The team adds curiosity driven knowledge retrieval, so the agent seeks facts when it feels a gap.

Curiosity here is a working rule: notice the gap, go fetch, then act. It was shown at the ACM Web Conference. Agents that fetch what they lack, at the moment they lack it, should handle unseen apps far better than agents frozen at training time.
arxiv-2601-19806:
Nuno Crokidakis and Lucas Sigaud model how racist content spreads through a population. They treat the spread like an epidemic, with three states for individuals. People can be susceptible, actively spreading, or opposed to the content. Transitions between states are driven by interactions, echoing how views pass between contacts, especially online.

The model shows phase transitions, sharp shifts between a society where the content dies out and one where it persists. Such thresholds depend on how strongly interactions push people between states. Online networks amplify the dynamics the model captures. Understanding the tipping points could inform moderation and education strategies. The work applies tools from statistical physics to a social harm.
arxiv-2601-20106:
Shamse Tasnim Cynthia, Joy Krishan Das, and Banani Roy ask whether all software developers use AI coding agents in the same way. Their 2026 study compares core developers, who sit near the center of a project, with peripheral developers, who contribute less often. Earlier work showed that the two groups adopt AI tools at different rates.

The authors study how that gap plays out now that coding agents can act on their own. The question matters because agents are changing how teams divide work and review code. If core and peripheral developers use agents in unlike ways, project leads may need unlike rules and support for each group.
arxiv-2601-20406:
S. Elgammal studies whether the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider could reveal a torsion field, an extension of gravity in Einstein-Cartan theory. The analysis uses privately simulated data matched to the collider's planned setup, with proton collisions at high energy. It focuses on pairs of muons with large mass.

The key variable is an angular distribution measured in the Collins-Soper frame. A torsion field would distort that distribution in a characteristic way. Case studies of this kind tell experimenters which signals to hunt for when the upgraded collider turns on. They also show how strong a signal must be to stand out.
arxiv-2601-20606:
Xinyu Wang and five colleagues present WFR-MFM, a one-step inference method for dynamic unbalanced optimal transport. Reconstructing how a system evolves from limited observations is fundamental in single-cell biology. There, unbalanced optimal transport models transport and mass change together, since cells divide and die as they move through states.

Existing approaches simulate trajectories at inference time, which makes inference a bottleneck at scale. A one-step method removes that simulation loop. Faster reconstruction would let biologists trace how cell populations develop across far larger datasets. The point is speed. A one-step read can stand in for a long run that few labs can pay for. It turns a slow step into a fast one, and that is no small thing.
arxiv-2601-20806:
Jiangen He and Wen Lou map how library and information science schools organize their research. Their 2026 study is the first full empirical map of its kind, they report. It covers schools across the United States. The team analyzed more than fourteen thousand publications. They came from over twelve hundred faculty members at forty-four institutions, across the years 2013 to 2024.

The authors used word embeddings and topic modeling to sort the work. They found sixteen distinct research themes. Those themes group into three broad dimensions. They are Library and Knowledge Organization, Human-Centered Technology, and Computing Systems. The map shows how each school's structure and portfolio fit together. It gives the field a clear view of where its strengths now lie.
arxiv-2601-21006:
Michael Jones and five co-authors fuse simulation and experiment to read fusion shots. Their 2026 paper concerns inertial confinement fusion, or ICF. A mix of physics-based simulation and experiments was key to reaching ignition in ICF. Both sides produce mixed outputs: scalars and images. Only part of the simulated data is available in real shots. That gap makes inference about a shot hard.

The authors propose a joint diffusion approach to multi-modal inference. Diffusion models can fill in missing views in a principled way. Trained across both data worlds, the model can infer hidden values. Better inference helps physicists tune the next shot. The work joins plasma physics with machine learning.
arxiv-2601-21106:
Annesh Pal and three co-authors make a flexible clustering model scale to wide data. Their 2026 paper studies Dirichlet process mixture models, or DPMMs. These models estimate the number of clusters from the data itself. They draw that number from an infinite choice of partitions. That freedom makes them a robust alternative to parametric mixtures. The catch is cost: inference in high dimensions is heavy. Two key parameters are usually fixed by hand.

The authors let both the concentration parameter and the variance be unknown. Their adaptive model learns them from the data. Collapsed variational inference keeps the computation tractable. Scaling such models matters for modern datasets with many features. The paper targets clustering that adapts its own complexity. It serves analysts who cannot guess cluster counts in advance.
arxiv-2601-21206:
Yu Guo and Rong-Xin Miao study a web of linked theories in holography, the idea that a bulk world can be described by a theory on its edge. Their setup joins several such edge theories through branches of a curved gravity model. Each branch carries its own coupling strength.

Using a classic theorem recast for holography, the authors prove a junction rule on the joining surface. That rule leads to conservation laws at the nodes of the web. The work also links the setup to parallel worlds that a signal could pass through. It gives a cleaner picture of how linked holographic systems share energy and information.
arxiv-2601-21306:
Wei-Di Chang, Mikael Henaff, Brandon Amos, Gregory Dudek, and Scott Fujimoto question a basic belief about model-based reinforcement learning. The usual story blames weak long-term forecasts and piling errors for poor results. Planning by search, on that view, should fix a learned policy.

The authors find that search can hurt results even when the model is highly accurate. Swapping a learned policy for search is not a plug-and-play upgrade. Something about the search itself clashes with how the policy was trained. The finding urges care: a good world model does not guarantee that planning on top of it will help.
arxiv-2601-21506:
Joonhee Lee, Hyunseung Shin, and JeongGil Ko design a navigation system for indoor robots that pairs speed with understanding. Classic mapping methods locate a robot reliably but need detailed maps. They also cannot read the signs and room numbers that guide people indoors.

Vision-language models can read those cues but often react too slowly for a moving robot. The authors combine both strengths in a dual-process design. A fast process keeps the robot moving safely, while a slower one reads the scene for meaning. The pairing targets hospitals, offices, and malls, where robots must move quickly and still find the right door.
arxiv-2601-21706:
Nan Lin, Yanbo Wang, and Jacco Heres unify generative tasks for smart meter data under one flow-based model. Meter data underpin planning and running the distribution grid. Privacy rules often make the real data unavailable, and what is collected can be corrupted or too coarse.

A generative model can fill those gaps with realistic synthetic series. Flow matching gives one frame for tasks like imputation, upscaling, and scenario creation. Grid planners could then test plans against rich synthetic demand without touching private records. The unified design also cuts the need for a separate tool per task.
arxiv-2601-21806:
Walter Wreszinski revisits one of the oldest puzzles in quantum mechanics, the EPR paradox. The paradox was meant to show that quantum theory must be incomplete if it respects locality. Locality is the idea that distant objects cannot instantly affect each other. Generations of debate followed about what the theory really says.

In his 2026 preprint, Wreszinski draws out a principle he finds implicit in a 1935 paper by Schrödinger. Using it, he argues for a proof that the EPR-locality paradox does not arise within the Copenhagen interpretation. He shows the point already with the simplest case, an entangled pair of two spin one-half particles. The claim, if it holds, would settle a long conceptual dispute about where the paradox actually lives.
arxiv-2601-22006:
Vasily Bokov, Lisa Kohl, Sebastian Schmitt, and Vedran Dunjko ask how little quantum computing is enough. Quantum machine learning is often sold as a promising use for quantum computers, backed by proofs of possible advantage. The authors invert the usual question: how small a role can the quantum device play while the advantage survives?

Their 2026 preprint studies learning under quantum priors, where most of the work is classical and the quantum part is minimal. Proving advantages in that lean setting matters because near-term quantum hardware is scarce and error-prone. If a small quantum contribution still provably helps, useful quantum learning could arrive years earlier than designs that need a full quantum pipeline.
arxiv-2601-22206:
Shi Bo and AmirEmad Ghassami study imitation learning when the student cannot see the world cleanly. In offline imitation, an agent learns from recorded expert behavior. Trouble starts when part of the state that drove the expert's decisions is observed only through noisy measurements, and the distribution shifts before deployment.

Those flaws create spurious links between states and actions. Standard behavioral cloning then converges to systematically wrong behavior, whether it uses the raw measurements or ignores them. The authors' 2026 preprint develops causal imitation learning that corrects for measurement error and distribution shift. The problem is practical: robots and medical policies alike learn from sensors that never report the true state.
arxiv-2601-22506:
Kaili Sun and four co-authors show a surface that emits heat waves with a twist that flips by side. Metasurfaces are thin, patterned sheets that steer waves of many kinds. Their 2026 preprint reports Janus chirality: the emitted heat's spin turns one way on one face, the other way on the back.

Getting such coherent, two-faced emission from one device is a hard feat. The team show it in a real build, not just on paper. Control of heat glow's spin could serve sensing, signaling, and heat control. The work opens a new knob for thermal design.
arxiv-2601-22906:
P. H. Cezar and a team of astronomers report gas observations of six nearby quasars. These are type-2 quasars, bright galactic centers partly hidden from view, drawn from the QSOFEED sample. Using a near-infrared instrument on a large telescope in the Canary Islands, they took long-slit spectra of each one.

The spectra trace warm molecular gas plus atomic gas at low and high ionization. Such gas shows how quasar energy pushes back on its host galaxy, a process called feedback. Feedback helps explain how galaxies and their central black holes grow together.
arxiv-2601-23006:
Junyou Su and a team of co-authors pick better training data for fine-tuning language models. Training on full datasets is costly, and extra data often adds little. Existing selection methods are tied to one domain: what works for general instructions fails on reasoning, and the reverse also holds.

Their method, InstructDiff, uses differential entropy to judge data in a domain-adaptive way. Smarter selection could cut training bills while keeping quality high. It also makes fine-tuning feasible for smaller teams with narrow, specialized data. Domain-adaptive selection is the aim, since instruction data and reasoning data reward very different selection strategies.
arxiv-2601-23206:
Morten I. K. Munk, Arturo Valdivia, and Paolo Burelli generate dynamic game content with small language models. Large models promise rich, changing game worlds, but they suffer narrative incoherence and high running costs. Their size also forces cloud access, which offline games cannot assume.

The proof of concept shows small models can produce high-quality content locally. On-device generation keeps games playable without a connection and cuts server bills. It also keeps player data on the machine, a privacy plus for studios. Small models answer the offline problem directly, since they can run on the player's own machine without cloud access.
arxiv-2603-01506:
