pmc-13407506:
Qin Wang, Rundong Yang, and Qizhi Zhou studied, in 2026, where the tiny feet of an implanted eye lens end up sitting after surgery for short-sightedness. One month after implantation, ultrasound microscopy classified foot position in 80 patients, and the team compared eye measurements taken before surgery across the three landing zones.

Feet resting in the intended groove numbered 47 eyes, against 42 on the ciliary body and 38 tucked beneath it. Many measurements differed between groups at first pass, including chamber depth and lens thickness. After full adjustment, only three factors held up independently: older age, stronger short-sight prescription, and lens size, while apparent links with chamber volume and ciliary shape faded as likely confounding. Foot position also tracked closely with how far the lens vaulted forward.
pmc-13407806:
Febriana Rahmawati and co-authors build, in 2026, an antifungal ferrofluid from natural ingredients against a toxin-producing mould. Aspergillus flavus contaminates food worldwide. The team combined zinc oxide with copper ferrite and soursop leaf extract. Iron sand and coconut oil completed the mix. The result was magnetically responsive nanocomposites. Varying the ferrite-extract share tuned performance.

Crystal analysis confirmed two phases, zinc oxide and copper ferrite, in their expected structures, and leaf-extract chemistry showed on the particle surfaces. Adding extract shrank particles from about 52 to 23 nanometres and made them more uniform, which likely helped them cross fungal membranes. In plate tests run in triplicate, the fluids held the mould back with clear zones between 7.60 and 8.90 millimetres, growing wider as extract content rose. The authors credit both smaller size and leaf-derived bioactive compounds.
pmc-13407906:
Christopher W. Carson and co-authors argue, in 2026, that DNA sequence itself writes codes governing how gene switches meet the spools DNA wraps around. Most studies of transcription factors and nucleosomes focus on the proteins. The team, though, identified four distinct classes of nucleosomal DNA pattern. They include the classic alternating weak-strong letter pattern. All are widespread across the human genome in living cells and test tubes alike.

Nucleosomes sharing a pattern sit rotationally in phase, while different patterns sit at specific offsets, amounting to distinct positioning codes. Surveying 744 transcription factors across eukaryotes, the authors tied two pattern families to factor binding in chromatin, and a score comparing their proportions predicted nucleosome occupancy in vitro. Combining that score with real occupancy data revealed four distinct interaction modes around binding sites.
pmc-13408306:
Zian Pan, Guansan Zheng, Zixuan Xu, and Lei Yuan propose a 2026 design method for a new kind of movable antenna. It is aimed at very short, highly reliable wireless messages. Pinching antennas slide along a waveguide, so their positions can be tuned. Yet tuning them under collision limits and fading channels is a hard maths problem.

The team built a learning agent that works with angle-like phase values instead of raw coordinates. This sidesteps a wrap-around glitch that upsets training. The agent then maps its choices back to legal antenna positions. They also derived a tidy stats-based account of signal strength and error rates. A search routine trims packet length to the least a set reliability target allows. In tests, the scheme beat standard methods on rate, errors, and efficiency. The gains grew as more antennas shared one waveguide.
pmc-13408506:
Ripenmeet Salhotra writes in 2026 about the stubborn gap between India's courtroom rulings on end-of-life care and what happens in its intensive care units. A recent judgment reaffirmed that artificial nutrition and hydration may be withdrawn. A 2023 Supreme Court ruling also simplified the approval route, through primary and secondary medical boards. Yet the case in question was reportedly the first in three years to use that route. It moved only after a family petitioned the top court.

Salhotra warns that a protective framework can chill good practice when boards barely exist in most regions. Doctors who once decided with families in good faith may now fear that acting without formal approval looks unlawful. Advance directives raise the same tension. Patient autonomy is welcome and overdue, yet the machinery for honouring it stays patchy. The letter urges implementation, not just recognition.
pmc-13408606:
Sandhiya Vijayabaskaran and Sen Cheng model in 2026 how an animal might combine what it sees with an internal sense of where its goal lies. Navigation in uncertain surroundings demands exactly that juggling, and engineers usually assume more signals always help. Their deep reinforcement learning agent learned to navigate using both a visual signal and a goal-vector signal, each with adjustable noise.

How noisy each signal was dictated how much the agent leaned on each source and how its internal spatial maps formed. Keeping the ability to use either signal alone, not just the blend, proved crucial when conditions changed. Counter-intuitively, dropping one signal sometimes improved performance when the remaining signal was trustworthy, though the agent became fragile. The work warns biologists that redundant sensing in animals is subtler than sensor fusion in machines.
pmc-13408706:
Branham Kitoko and colleagues sampled imported poultry in Kinshasa in 2026 and found worrying levels of drug resistance in gut bacteria before the birds even reached farms. Most day-old chicks and hatching eggs for the capital's mid-sized sector arrive by air from abroad, a legal trade that could also import resistant microbes. Five importers and hatcheries joined the study across five incoming batches from Belgium, Zambia, and an unnamed source.

Every chick sample carried Escherichia coli. Resistance testing showed roughly three quarters of isolates resisting amoxicillin and the common sulfonamide pairing, and over two thirds resisting ampicillin, while some other antibiotics still worked well. Because these birds seed local production, the authors frame imported stock as a watch point: screening at entry could catch resistance before it spreads through Congolese poultry and on to consumers.
pmc-13408906:
Fabian Kananen, Hannes Bode, Miina Ollikainen, and Ilkka Immonen exploit a natural experiment in 2026: identical twins who differ in eye disease. Age-related macular degeneration runs in families yet also responds to environment, and chemical methylation marks on DNA are one route by which environment might act. Twenty-nine Finnish twin pairs, one twin with worse disease than the other, gave blood for genome-wide methylation reading.

Nearly ten thousand measured sites inside known candidate genes were compared within pairs, a design that cancels genetics, sex, age, and shared childhood. One site reached statistical significance but its difference was too small to meet the team's own bar for biological relevance, and no site cleared both bars. The authors conclude that blood carries no large methylation signal at these loci, while allowing that subtle effects could hide below what twenty-nine pairs can detect.
pmc-13409006:
Felix Wohlrab and a large neuroimmunology team test in 2026 whether a finger-prick style dried plasma spot can stand in for frozen blood samples when measuring a marker of astrocyte injury. The protein, GFAP, rises in neuromyelitis optica, an autoimmune disease attacking optic nerves and spinal cord. Seventy participants, including patients with three related diseases and healthy controls, gave paired samples during remission.

An ultrasensitive assay read the dried spots, and results correlated strongly with measurements from conventional plasma across all groups. In the neuromyelitis group, values also agreed well with a reference serum method, and the marker related to disability measures. Dried spots would let clinics mail samples without freezers, widening access to biomarker testing for remote patients. The authors present the approach as a practical route to decentralised monitoring.
pmc-13410606:
Misako Suto and co-authors describe in 2026 a hospital protocol for sudden massive bleeding during surgery, called SUTO. Heavy bleeding demands many jobs at once: steadying circulation, finding the source, bringing blood products, and calling in extra teams. A rehearsed plan keeps those jobs from colliding.

Roles, activation steps, and supply carts are set in advance, with charts posted at each operating room door. Teams practice in real rooms with real gear before any crisis. One real case put the system to work when a splenic artery tore during cancer surgery near the stomach. The report, the first in English on the protocol, aims to help other hospitals build their own versions.
pmc-13411906:
Maryam Ghadimi and co-authors publish a 2026 protocol for a planned review of ways to prevent a rare eye infection after injections into the eye. Such injections are common in retinal care, yet a small share of patients develop endophthalmitis, an infection that can threaten sight. Clinics mix preventive steps in varied combinations, and earlier reviews judged each step on its own.

The team will search five databases for trials and observational studies in adults, with paired reviewers screening studies and grading their quality. Planned comparisons use network meta-analysis, which ranks combined strategies against each other rather than one at a time. Outcomes include confirmed infection, need for surgery, and sharpness of vision.
pmc-13413006:
Jacek Kubica and colleagues review in 2026 where vericiguat, a newer heart failure drug, fits beside the four standard pillars of treatment. The drug stimulates an enzyme pathway that stiff vessels and scarred heart muscle lose, offering a mechanism distinct from existing medicines. Trials, subgroup analyses, and fresh real-world data were weighed, with attention to patients whose condition recently worsened despite standard therapy.

Vericiguat trimmed heart failure outcomes modestly, with the clearest gains in high-risk patients after a recent decompensation episode. A newer program in stable outpatients missed its main endpoint yet kept a favourable safety profile. The authors frame the drug as a risk-targeted add-on for selected patients who still carry residual risk, not a replacement for cornerstone therapy.
pmc-13414306:
Mayane Cristina Pereira Marques and co-authors explore in 2026 whether the iron-chelator deferoxamine could interfere with how uropathogenic E. coli feeds on iron. People with neurogenic bladder, who cannot void properly, suffer repeated urinary infections, and bacterial iron uptake is a tempting drug target. Rats with severed spinal cords supplied a living model; their urine grew E. coli, and computer docking then tested how the drug and its iron-loaded form fit the bacterium's uptake receptor.

The drug complex settled plausibly into the receptor's recognition pocket, with binding scores suggesting weak-to-moderate fit against reference molecules. The authors stress this is structural suggestion, not proof of blocked feeding, since bacteria run several iron systems in parallel. Live dosing and uptake experiments top their list of next steps.
pmc-13414506:
Reuven Yosef reviews in 2026 the infections children can catch from domestic cats, balancing the animals' real comforts against their role as pathogen carriers. Toddlers hug cats, share sandboxes, and wash hands imperfectly, raising exposure to parasites, bacteria, fungi, and flea-borne agents. The synthesis walks through the major culprits, from Toxoplasma and Toxocara worms to cat-scratch Bartonella, ringworm, and rabies, detailing routes, symptoms, and who faces the worst risk.

Pregnant women and immunocompromised people join children at the sharp end of risk across the cases reviewed. Urban cat management, including feeding colonies and trap-neuter-return programs, shapes how much contact children get. Practical defences centre on hygiene, regular veterinary care, and teaching caregivers, framed by a One Health view linking homes, streets, and clinics.
pmc-13415506:
Dana Pietsch and colleagues published this correction in 2026 for their Scientific Reports article on buried soils from a humid Holocene period in Wadi Shuwayhi, Oman. Errors had crept into Figures 7 and 8, whose legends were wrong, with Figure 7 duplicating Figure 8. Parts of the reference list also needed repair.

The notice prints full replacement legends describing microscope features of two soil horizons, including limestone fragments, bone bits, gypsum deposits, and root remains in voids. Figure 7 itself is replaced in the updated article. A corrected geological map reference follows. Readers now get the intended images and captions for the soil evidence.
pmc-13415706:
Yongfei Fan and co-authors issued this correction in 2026 for their Nano-Micro Letters article on copper based nanocatalytic therapy for non-small cell lung cancer. Several fixes were needed. The full name behind the abbreviation DMSA was written wrongly at its first appearances across the article and supplement.

A chemical equation in the contents graphic and first figure also needed correction, giving the proper reaction between copper ions and hydrogen peroxide. During figure assembly, a statistics plot for one cell line was accidentally duplicated from another line's plot. Replacement graphics and figures are supplied, plus an updated supplement. The authors state the final conclusions stay unaffected.
pmc-13415806:
Jing Zhang, Beifang Wang, and Duo Zhou simplify how coal mines judge rockburst risk, in a 2026 study. Rockbursts are sudden, violent releases of stored energy in coal seams that wreck roadways and endanger miners. Existing risk systems use many overlapping factors that blur judgment. Their factor reduction method analyzes seven candidate factors mathematically and in the field.

Three factors dominated: changes in coal seam thickness, geological structures, and floor coal thickness. A trial at the Yadian coal mine in Shaanxi matched real conditions on the ground. Sorted prevention measures follow the risk classes. The work aims at sharper early warning for a hazard growing as mines deepen.
pmc-13416006:
Ibiebele and colleagues check what steroids given before a preterm birth do for mothers with diabetes and their babies. The drugs spread on shaky evidence. The steroids speed fetal lung maturity but can disturb blood sugar. Their 2026 study follows 5,067 women who gave birth from thirty five weeks in two New South Wales districts. It compares mothers with diabetes who did or did not get steroids, and mothers without diabetes who did.

Between the two diabetes groups, outcomes did not differ. No gain for mothers or babies showed up in the records. Against steroid treated mothers without diabetes, the diabetes group faced higher risks of low blood sugar. The adjusted relative risk was 1.61 in the model. Nursery or intensive care admission ran higher. The authors conclude benefit at late preterm gestation remains unproven for this group. Follow up studies are needed before routine use hardens into habit.
pmc-13418506:
Jose G Anguiano-Hernandez and colleagues ask what drives foot warming during walking, in a 2026 physiology study. Twenty one healthy young adults walked for ten minutes on level, uphill, and downhill slopes at a set speed. Leg blood flow and tissue oxygen saturation were measured in thigh, calf, and foot before and after each walk, alongside foot temperature.

Uphill walking raised leg blood flow most and drew down muscle oxygen saturation, matching harder work. Foot temperature change tracked only with oxygen saturation in the foot itself, not with leg flow or working muscle measures. Skin blood flow, sweat, and air cooling are the likely missing drivers, the authors suggest.
pmc-13418606:
Yeni Arroyave-Guerrero and colleagues recount a rare lung tumour long mistaken for asthma, in a 2026 case report. A 75 year old woman had eight years of breathlessness, cough, and wheeze unrelieved by inhalers, with repeated pneumonias. Scans showed a growth near the left lung root blocking airways, yet several biopsy attempts gave no diagnosis.

Surgical exploration found a localised tumour inside the lower lobe bronchus. Removing that lobe with a sleeve technique spared the upper lobe and avoided taking the whole lung. Pathology confirmed a low grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma with clear margins and no node spread. Recovery was favourable.
pmc-13418706:
Lihua Fang, Yueru Yao, Jinmei Wu, and Jie Ning review virulence of Streptococcus suis serotype 2, a pig pathogen that also infects people, in a 2026 article. The bacterium causes meningitis, blood poisoning, and a toxic shock like syndrome with high death rates. The review follows infection from colonisation through blood survival, immune evasion, and brain barrier crossing.

Control systems and effector tools are dissected, from capsule and pili to metal grabbing systems and a pore forming toxin. Disputed roles for several factors get a dedicated airing. Vaccine candidates and antivirulence targets are weighed, with a plea for natural route pig models over mouse shortcuts.
pmc-13420306:
Takamine and colleagues test whether exercise can undo what a fatty diet does to growing bone, focusing on fat inside the marrow. Their 2026 study splits male mice into four groups: normal or high fat feed, crossed with rest or treadmill running. Running lasts thirty minutes a day, five days a week, for sixteen weeks. Density, strength, and turnover markers are assayed.

The fat fed mice gained weight and marrow fat, and running trimmed the weight gain but not the marrow fat. A marker of bone breakdown rose on the fatty diet and exercise did not pull it back, while a bone building marker rose only in runners. Adjusted for body weight, bone density ran lower in fat fed mice and higher in exercised ones, with no interaction. Running helps the scale, the authors conclude, but marrow fat from a rich diet stays put.
pmc-13421206:
Boon-Kok Tan surveys, in a 2026 review, the prospects and obstacles for the next generation of astronomical receivers that detect sub-millimetre and terahertz waves from space. Heterodyne receivers, which shift faint cosmic signals to lower frequencies for analysis, sit at the heart of the telescopes he discusses.

Mixers based on superconductors anchor the designs he presents. They include ultra-broadband versions and compact receivers that split two signal bands at once. Focal plane arrays could grow to hundreds or thousands of pixels, speeding up sky mapping. He also introduces receivers that observe several bands simultaneously by reconfiguring standard layouts. The intended beneficiaries include upgrades to ALMA and planned facilities such as AtLAST, alongside future space missions.
pmc-13421506:
Janna Eilts leads a ten-author team combining two microscopy tricks, in a 2026 paper, to photograph the cell's own protein machinery at nanometre detail. Super-resolution microscopes can now locate single molecules precisely, yet sparse labelling of unmodified cells wastes that precision.

Their method embeds labelled samples in a specially homogenised gel that expands them seven to eight fold, then images them with single-molecule microscopy. The expansion raises labelling density enough to resolve the eight-nanometre spacing of tubulin building blocks in microtubules and the cage pattern of clathrin-coated pits. Two-colour imaging in neurons revealed ring-shaped active-zone structures some 44 to 48 nanometres across. The authors offer the technique for studying natural protein complexes with no genetic changes.
pmc-13422106:
Gertel and colleagues searched urine in 2026 for a non-invasive test for endometriosis, a painful condition where womb-like tissue grows outside the womb. Diagnosis often needs surgery, and delays average years. The team compared urine proteins from 73 women with surgically confirmed disease and 73 matched women without it.

A protein called epidermal growth factor, or EGF, was clearly lower in urine from women with endometriosis. Above a set cutoff, the test correctly ruled out disease in about 94 in 100 cases. The rule-out power rose further in women who also reported pelvic pain outside their periods. The authors present urinary EGF as a candidate marker that could speed diagnosis without surgery. They note the test is better at ruling disease out than ruling it in.
pmc-13422706:
Motherwell and colleagues deliver a negative result in this 2026 animal study, testing whether an approved antifibrotic drug could rescue muscle lost to catastrophic injury. Volumetric muscle loss, where a chunk of muscle is destroyed, heals with dense scar instead of contractile tissue. Twelve pigs received such injuries in a leg muscle, with half then dosed daily with oral pirfenidone.

The drug behaved as its anti-inflammatory reputation promised at the gene level, quieting key fibrosis-driving signals including TNF and two chemokines. Yet at four weeks it had not reduced total collagen in the wound, measured two independent ways, though the scar's fibers were less densely packed. Worse, treated pigs recovered less contractile force and stopped gaining weight normally. The authors warn that systemic antifibrotics may sabotage the very recovery they aim to help, and dosing strategy needs rethinking.
pmc-13423506:
Cui and co-authors unveil a light-controlled platform for moving tiny objects around on an open surface, in this 2026 study. The surface has no patterned electrodes. A near-infrared laser melts a paraffin layer at one spot. That flips local charge transport from sluggish diffusion to flowing convection. It also builds a sharp electric-field gradient. The gradient grabs charged droplets through corona discharge. That is the same effect that makes high-voltage wires crackle.

A single steerable beam transported droplets, solid particles, and gas bubbles, and performed the full microfluidic repertoire: moving, merging, splitting, dispensing, and steering reactions. The surface kept working tilted, vertical, upside down, and curved, and handled volumes spanning roughly ten orders of magnitude, from picoliters to milliliters, including corrosive liquids and biological samples. The authors pitch the design as a simple, unified route to programmable lab-on-a-chip systems.
pmc-13424106:
Feron and co-authors document a sharp turn in European wildfire risk in this 2026 climate study. For decades, ignitions and burned area declined. Recent seasons, including a record-breaking 2025, have overwhelmed firefighting capacity across southern Europe. The team asked whether the weather itself has become more fire-prone.

Combining national fire statistics with atmospheric reanalysis data, they found summer days with extreme fire weather have more than doubled. That shift spans 1981 to 2025. It covers vast parts of the Iberian Peninsula, France, Italy, and Greece. The shift tracks broader warming and drying patterns in the region. Year-to-year swings in fire risk also lined up with two great climate patterns, the North Atlantic Oscillation and the El Niño Southern Oscillation, hinting that seasonal outlooks could anticipate bad years. The authors call for adaptation strategies built for the new regime.
pmc-13426206:
Abdulla Al Mamun Bhuyan and colleagues tested whether the anticancer drug tasisulam kills red blood cells ahead of schedule in a 2026 laboratory study. Tasisulam promotes programmed death in tumor cells and is in trials for lung cancer, lymphoma, breast cancer, melanoma, and other tumors, yet anemia is a known adverse effect. The suspected route is eryptosis, premature red cell shrinkage with phosphatidylserine flipped to the surface.

Human red cells at low concentration were incubated with tasisulam doses of 75 and 150 units and checked for calcium rise, oxidative stress, ceramide build-up, and kinase or caspase activity. Defining that signaling helps explain drug-related anemia and suggests protective countermeasures.
pmc-13426406:
Dodd-o and colleagues reported in 2026 on a peptide gel designed to grow new blood vessels where tissue needs better blood supply. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, and these ones join on their own into tiny fibres. One peptide mimics a growth signal called VEGF that tells vessel cells to multiply, while a second, stronger peptide gives the gel its structure and firmness.

Dodd-o tuned the gel stiffness across a wide range while keeping the signal peptide able to reach its receptor on vessel cells. Computer simulations and magnetic resonance tests showed the two parts pack closely without blocking the active signal. In cell tests the gels sped up vessel cell growth, and in mouse and rat implants they drew in new vessels that linked stably with the host tissue. The design offers a flexible platform for building healing materials.
pmc-13426506:
Hyewon Jeon and colleagues review stimuli-responsive, cell-mimicking vesicles for drug delivery in a 2026 pharmaceutical article. Vesicles can carry both water-loving and fat-loving drugs together, enabling combination therapy, yet ordinary carriers accumulate poorly at targets and spread nonspecifically. Adding responses to cues such as pH, enzymes, or light allows controlled release at the right place and time with less body-wide toxicity.

Newer designs go further, acting as artificial cells that can synthesize compounds on site, react to signals, and communicate with living cells. The review argues vesicle engineering is moving from passive transport toward programmable therapeutic platforms.
pmc-13428106:
Apiliogullari and colleagues tested in 2026 whether blood markers can quickly identify intracerebral hemorrhage, bleeding inside the brain, where fast diagnosis shapes treatment and survival. Scans confirm the diagnosis but take time and access. The team measured four brain proteins in blood, plus several hormone signals, in patients and healthy volunteers.

Samples came from 71 patients with scan-confirmed bleeding and 30 healthy controls, repeated over two weeks. All four brain markers separated patients from controls at every time point. One marker, GFAP, a protein from support cells, was far higher in patients on day one, by orders of magnitude. Two hormone signals also ran higher in patients, and marker levels did not differ by age group. The authors present the panel as promising but caution that telling one stroke type from another still needs study.
pmc-13428706:
Mthembu and colleagues use modeling to test whether ring shaped peptides can jam a chaperone the malaria parasite needs to survive stress. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, leans on Grp78, a folding helper in its protein workshop, when drugs batter it. Two peptide families, gramicidin S and the tyrocidines, already kill the parasite. Their 2026 study docks these rings onto the chaperone's structure and runs simulations to see where they stick and what they change.

The peptides settled on a patch of the chaperone's substrate binding part, spanning its arch and pocket. Human versions use other spots. Long simulations kept them bound. The fit looked like a conformational lock: the chaperone loses the flexing its work cycle needs. The rings also favored the parasite's workshop chaperone over its cytosolic cousin and over human counterparts. All results are predictions, the authors stress, awaiting wet lab proof.
pmc-13429006:
Marcello Arca and a large team trace, in a 2026 study, how fat particles move through the blood of people born without a key regulator protein. ANGPTL3 normally slows the breakdown of triglyceride-rich particles, and people lacking it enjoy lifelong low blood fats and less heart disease. The team studied three people with no working copy of the gene, four with one copy, and ten matched controls. Tracer methods followed fat transport after meals across particle types.

Production of the particles ran at normal speed in everyone. In those with complete deficiency, breakdown ran astonishingly fast, clearing particles in minutes instead of hours. Their LDL particles, the cholesterol carriers tied to heart risk, came out oddly composed yet were cleared faster too. Half-deficiency gave a milder speed-up. Drug developers mimicking this state gain a detailed picture of what to expect and watch for.
pmc-13429106:
Daniel J. Davis and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether stiffer shoe soles can repay some of the energy older walkers lose. Aging shifts walking work from the ankle toward the hip, and slopes make the deficit worse. Nineteen volunteers around age 70 walked under several slope conditions wearing shoes fitted with carbon fiber insoles of rising stiffness. Joint motions, forces, and breathing costs were measured throughout.

Stiffer soles cut energy lost at the front of the foot but raised losses at the heel, leaving whole-foot results mixed. Peak ankle effort rose about 10 percent in the stiffest shoes. Knee and hip mechanics barely changed, and overall energy cost showed no consistent saving. The authors float a different hope: stronger ankle demand might train calf muscles over time. Footwear designers get precise limits on what a flat stiff insole can do.
pmc-13430206:
Franz Felix Konen leads a large German team testing, in a 2026 study, whether updated multiple sclerosis rules can be applied with ordinary hospital tools. The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria lets doctors diagnose MS earlier by counting the optic nerve as a fifth site and by accepting certain spinal fluid markers. The study enrolled 215 adults after a first suspected demyelinating event or with silent MRI lesions, worked up the standard way between 2020 and 2025.

Under the new rules about 94 percent met the diagnosis at the first assessment, against about 84 percent under the older rules. Optic nerve evidence supplied most of the extra diagnoses, and reclassifying silent-lesion cases supplied most of the rest. An electrical eye test caught optic nerve involvement in about 89 percent of cases. Newer MRI markers were not even needed for the gain shown.
pmc-13431006:
Shilling and colleagues further tested in 2026 a questionnaire that measures how cancer and its treatment disrupt patients' everyday roles, such as caregiving and money duties. The scale was first built for advanced cancer, but its makers meant it for all cancers and stages. This study checked it in people treated with curative intent, three years after diagnosis.

The data came from 1,077 survivors of breast, gynecological, and blood cancers in a long-running British cohort. The sixteen-item scale held together well, and its subscales were mostly sound. Scores lined up with related measures of work, social life, and quality of life in the pattern predicted. A statistical model confirmed the scale's three-part structure, though its parts overlapped more than expected. The authors conclude the scale is fit for wider use in survivorship research.
pmc-13431306:
Li and colleagues tracked gut microbes in Hu sheep lambs in 2026 through diarrhea and antibiotic treatment, using gene sequencing of feces. They compared lambs in early diarrhea, lambs in late recovery after a four-drug treatment mix, and healthy lambs, rebuilding hundreds of microbial genomes from the sequence data.

They assembled 482 high-quality genomes, most from the three phyla typical of ruminant guts. In early diarrhea, usually friendly bacteria carried more virulence genes. By late recovery the diarrhea had eased, yet resistance genes against two drug classes had grown, a leftover risk from the combined antibiotics. Two potential disease-causing genera also surged during diarrhea and carried hundreds of virulence genes each. The authors say antibiotic clearing of sensitive microbes, more than diarrhea itself, drove the deepest community change.
pmc-13432906:
Rashid Iqbal and colleagues sprayed quinoa leaves with two natural compounds to shield the crop from tellurium, a toxic element leaking into farm soils. Serotonin, a plant signal chemical, and allantoin, a protective nitrogen compound, were tested together under controlled plots.

Tellurium stress alone slashed growth and yield and raised cell damage markers in the plants. Sprayed together, the two compounds lifted grain yield by about 90 percent over stressed plants that got no spray. They also cut tellurium reaching the grain by about two thirds, keeping the harvested food safer. Soil microbe life and nutrient levels recovered as well, so Iqbal backs the spray pair for poisoned fields.
pmc-13434306:
Nathan F Bellis and coauthors detail in 2026 how a virus that infects gut bacteria throws its own copy enzyme into the host cell. The enzyme is huge, with about 3,500 building units in one chain. Two helper proteins leave with it to form a short lived entry machine.

Images of full and emptied virus shells show one helper forming a pore in the outer wall. The second helper builds a tunnel through the gap beyond the wall. A hub in the tail senses contact with the host and times the release. The loose chain form may let the huge enzyme thread a narrow channel.
pmc-13434606: Untalan, Pagote, and Tejero write to refine a Canadian ultra-processed food screener built on the NOVA classification. They flag self-reported intake as prone to recall bias. They urge adding food-environment indicators, such as source and affordability. They also suggest pairing NOVA categories with standard examples or nutrient markers. That would fix inconsistent boundaries. They close by recommending the screener be embedded in existing public health systems for policy impact.
pmc-13437206:
Sung Ho Hwang, writing in 2026, asks why heart artery CT scans expose patients in poorer countries to far more radiation than in rich ones. A world study of 19,302 patients in 101 countries found doses about twice as high in low-income settings, and the median African dose ran over five times the Western European level.

Newer scanners cut dose by over a fifth, yet doses stayed far higher in poor countries even after machine type was weighed. How well teams tune their settings and run the scan matters just as much. Low tube voltage, scans timed to the heartbeat, and smarter image rebuilding can each trim exposure. New deep learning rebuilding alone has cut dose by forty to sixty percent without blurring detail in cited studies. The piece argues training, careful patient setup, and shared know-how must travel with the hardware if dose gaps are to close.
pmc-13437506:
Andrea Gonsek and colleagues recorded brain activity in stick insects to learn how a night-active animal sorts smell from touch and sound. In darkness, the stick insect leans on its long antennae, feeling obstacles up close and catching scent and air movement from afar. Their 2026 study set up long-term recordings from many neurons at once in the antennal lobe, the brain's first smell station.

Hexanal, the smell of freshly cut leaves and a food cue for this leaf eater, lit a distinct pattern across the network. Mechanical stimulation, likely standing in for airborne vibration such as sound, also drove cells in the same region. A large share of neurons answered both kinds of input, showing the lobe is no pure smell center. The team frames the work as a first step toward using the stick insect to model how near-range touch and far-range scent merge.
pmc-13437906:
Surender and colleagues screened the whole genome in 2026 to find genes that sway how glioma, a brain tumor, responds to CDK4/6 blockers, drugs that halt cell division machinery. These drugs have disappointed in glioblastoma, so partners that sensitize or protect tumors are prized. Using CRISPR gene cutting and gene activation across five human glioma cell lines, the team hunted for modifiers, then checked the hits in cultures and in animals.

Losing a gene called AMBRA1 or boosting CCNE1 made cells resist the blockers. Breaking CHEK1 or FAM122A turned lethal only when the blockers were present, a pattern called synthetic lethality. Cells lacking AMBRA1 became extra sensitive to checkpoint kinase blockade, exposing a tailored weakness. Pairing a CHK1 blocker with a CDK4/6 blocker killed glioma cells in synergy in dishes, in patient-derived cultures, and in animals. The authors propose the pairing for glioblastoma trials.
pmc-13438106:
Soliman and colleagues design a fresh family of compounds that both attack bacteria and shield antibiotics from bacterial defense enzymes. Beta lactamase enzymes break penicillin type drugs, a core driver of drug resistance. Their 2026 study builds a series of dihydropyrimidinones, ring shaped molecules. It tests them against two Gram positive and one Gram negative bacterial species, then against resistant strains and the purified defense enzyme.

Most compounds showed moderate bacteria killing next to the standard drug amoxicillin. pmc-13439706:
Dai and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the human evidence for transmission ratio distortion, the bending of Mendel's rule that each parent passes either gene copy with equal odds. Distortion is well proven in other species, where selfish elements hijack reproduction, but human claims were scattered. The team gathered reports from the nineteen seventies through 2025 that met set criteria.

Ninety-six studies covering forty-two variants, genes, or regions qualified. Taken together they offered only preliminary and often conflicting evidence, and the methods shared repeated biases such as small samples and selective reporting. pmc-13441506:

pmc-13443106:

pmc-13443206:

pmc-13443306:

pmc-13444506:

pmc-13446306:

pmc-13447206:

pmc-13447906:

pmc-13448206:

pmc-13448306:

pmc-13448906:

pmc-13449506:

pmc-13449806:

pmc-13449906:
Wang and co-authors catalogue the imaging of a rare tumour that grows inside veins. Their 2026 retrospective series reviews nineteen cases of intravenous leiomyomatosis. pmc-13451606:

pmc-13451806:

pmc-13451906:

pmc-13452006:

pmc-13452206:

pmc-13452306:

pmc-13452406:

pmc-13452506:

pmc-13453306:

pmc-13453506:

pmc-13454206:

pmc-13455106:

pmc-13455506:

pmc-13457006:

pmc-13459606:

pmc-13461106:

pmc-13461506:

pmc-13461606:

pmc-13461706:

pmc-13461806:

pmc-13461906:

pmc-13462006:

pmc-13463506:

pmc-13463606:
David Huang and a large team ask whether hormone-primed IVF cycles change the womb lining in ways that raise blood pressure risk in pregnancy. Clinics often prime the lining with hormones rather than relying on a natural cycle. The team built a single-cell map of lining tissue from both kinds of cycle.

Primed linings differed clearly at the gene level, with fewer uterine natural killer cells and weaker signals for embryo settling and blood vessel growth. Yet in 548 tracked pregnancies, primed-cycle conceptions showed no early imbalance in vessel growth markers and no extra cases of high blood pressure disorders. The womb, the authors argue, adapts well despite the early shifts.
pmc-13463806:
Yiheng Jiang and nine colleagues published this 2026 study developing a green ultrasound-assisted extraction for polysaccharides from Banqiao Codonopsis root, a prized Chinese medicine-food plant, and testing the product against ulcerative colitis. The standard hot-water method is slow, hot and wasteful, degrading the very compounds it extracts. The team optimised the ultrasound process statistically, probed how cavitation frees them, and compared yield and energy use against the conventional method.

At the optimum, 400 watts for 34 minutes, the ultrasound process yielded 21.31 percent polysaccharide, beating hot water by 42 percent, while cutting extraction time by 43.5 percent, energy use by 38.8 percent and carbon emissions by 56.9 percent, and stripping protein and nucleic acid waste more effectively. Ultrasound shrank the plant particles by about 22 percent and loosened the cellulose structure, easing their release. The authors present the method as the scalable, low-carbon route to producing this anti-inflammatory ingredient for functional foods and medicines.
pmc-13464506:
Gerlin and colleagues model the food fight between a bacterium and a tomato plant in this 2026 paper. The bacterium Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum causes bacterial wilt, a destructive crop disease. During infection the two organisms compete directly for nutrients. The team merged a genome scale metabolic model of the bacterium with one of the whole plant, then tuned it with experimental data.

Simulations predicted the flows of matter through the infected plant. The plant's photosynthesis limited bacterial growth more strongly than its mineral supply did. Falling water flow through the plant first slowed plant growth and later starved the bacteria. The bacterium also appeared to steal resources through the stem, though only to a limited degree. Gerlin highlights water flow as central to how this disease develops.
pmc-13465006:
Sang-Ho Jeong and three co-authors review bleeding care for gastric cancer, where tumor bleeding can kill quickly and stall all other treatment. Two decades of evidence feed a stepwise plan guided by how stable the patient's circulation is. Scope-based stopping of the bleed comes first in the plan.

For unstable patients or failed scope work, artery blocking through a catheter takes over. Palliative radiation offers a non-invasive route that can slow tumor bleeding over days. Surgery waits as the last resort when other routes fail. The review reframes success: halting the bleed only opens the gate, and survival turns on getting patients back to cancer therapy fast.
pmc-13465406:
Chatterjee and co-authors investigated a 2026 regulator of disc degeneration, the enzyme PHLPP1, in the nucleus pulposus, the gel centre of spinal discs. Degeneration there drives disc related low back pain through inflammation and matrix breakdown. Earlier work tied higher PHLPP1 levels to worse degeneration in patients.

In aged mice lacking the gene, age related disc degeneration and inflammation were blunted, most clearly in males, Chatterjee reports. Silencing the gene in degenerated human disc cells sharply suppressed inflammatory and signal recruiting genes such as IL1B, IL6, and several chemokines. Matrix building gene activity rose at the same time, shifting cells toward a less destructive, less tissue eating state overall. The authors position PHLPP1 as an upstream regulator of the disc's inflammatory networks and a candidate drug target for slowing degeneration.
pmc-13465606:
Charles Tremblay and co-authors report early work, published in 2026, on steering drug-loaded bacteria through tumors with magnets as a cancer treatment. The bacteria move on their own and can be guided, which sets the approach apart from a simple drug injection into a tumor. Reaching deep sites such as the pancreas and rectum needs image guidance inside a new magnetic setup.

The team lays out a full guided workflow, using endoscopic ultrasound or scans through the skin to place the bacteria. They frame the report as the first complete version of this delivery chain, built to settle the technical questions that a first trial in people would raise. Pancreatic and rectal cancers are the target diseases throughout.
pmc-13466406:
Jiangtao Hu, Byoung Ryong Jeong, and Qichang Yang introduce a journal special issue, writing in 2026. Now in its second edition, the issue covers how plants respond to light at the cell and molecule level. Light feeds plants through photosynthesis, yet it also acts as a rich signal that times flowering and shapes growth, chemistry, and stress defense.

Six papers in the collection range from small RNA signaling in maize to pigment metabolism, hormone shifts, antioxidant defense, and protection of the photosynthetic machinery. Together they show light quality acting at many control levels at once. One maize study found a small RNA's free levels changing with light through binding to a partner protein rather than through new production.
pmc-13466506:
Vladislav Kozák and Jiří Vala review local approaches for predicting how cracks start and grow inside structural materials, in a 2026 article. Rather than treating a part as uniform, these methods zoom into the stressed zone near a notch or flaw and let the tiny local structure speak. Modern statistics join the finite element calculations that engineers already use.

Three material families anchor the examples: metals where cracks begin around inclusions or grain boundary particles, fiber composites with strong interfaces, and hybrids of the two. Two-scale simulations, where small-scale behavior feeds a whole-part model, get the most attention. The review weighs hierarchical schemes, where scales pass results one way, against concurrent ones.
pmc-13466806:
Yachen Liu, Xi Liu, Hongmeng Ma, and Wenxin Li report a lung cancer that changed its tissue type during targeted treatment, an extremely rare switch, in a 2026 case report. The patient, a forty-five-year-old woman, had two years of cough, sputum, and breathlessness. Her cancer began as lung adenocarcinoma carrying an ALK gene rearrangement, treated with drugs that block that signal.

Under treatment the tumor transformed into pulmonary mucoepidermoid carcinoma, a type that normally arises on its own and makes up under one percent of lung cancers. Change into small cell cancer after such drugs is known, but this destination is almost unheard of. No shared guideline covers the mechanism or best care, which the report aims to start filling.
pmc-13467006:
Erin Tresselt Murray and colleagues study how heart-lung bypass during children's heart surgery splits two neutrophil weapons in opposite directions, in a 2026 study. Thirty-nine children from one day to four years old gave blood before bypass and a day after it. Bypass sent neutrophil counts soaring more than fourfold.

One weapon, the enzyme elastase, poured out more strongly after bypass yet did not forecast organ damage. The other, web-like traps the cells cast to snare germs, fell sharply after bypass. Children whose cells answered weakly to a gentle trap trigger before surgery carried the risk signal instead. The split matters because blocking inflammation wholesale could block a useful arm along with a harmful one.
pmc-13469206:
Martinelli and co-authors reviewed in 2026 evidence tying hearing loss in old age to cognitive decline and dementia, under the title the sound of silence. Cognitive impairment affects about 6.5 percent of people over 65, with no treatment reversing it. Hearing loss rises steeply with age, up to 40 percent past 65 and 75 percent past 80. The review covers ear-level damage and the brain's central processing of sound, plus screening tests from questionnaires to sound-booth audiometry.

Several paths may link the two: straining to hear loads the brain's thinking budget, and deafness breeds social isolation, itself a dementia risk. Central processing faults grow more important in later stages of age-related loss. The practical message is hopeful: hearing aids may delay decline, not just ease disability, and they lighten caregiver burden by restoring communication. Paired with cognitive training, correction of hearing is presented as one of the few levers available for prevention.
pmc-13469906:
Alsanousi and Prabhu review ways to measure mental workload from body signals in this 2026 paper. Cognitive load, the mental effort a task demands, affects safety and learning in jobs like flying and surgery. Self-reports miss quick changes during a task. So the authors assessed signals that sensors can track without entering the body. These included heart activity, brain waves, eye movements, and skin conductance.

The review drew on 37 sources published between 2021 and early 2026, including 25 original studies. Heart measures appeared most often, in 16 of the 25 studies, followed by brain-wave recording in 11. Brain signals linked most directly to mental effort but were hard to use outside labs, while wearable-friendly signals reflected general arousal instead. The authors propose pairing complementary signals rather than relying on any single one.
pmc-13471506:
Tian and colleagues built a finer-grained way to record skin damage in anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease where skin ulcers can signal lung danger. Their 2026 retrospective study coded ulceration, itch, and scale across seven body regions in 339 patients, distilled from 513 screened at one center.

Simple presence of any ulcer already carried information: it was linked to depleted CD8 T cells with an odds ratio of 3.35 in the screening analysis, and each additional ulcer site added its own association at 1.43 per site. Location mattered too, since facial ulceration tied to pulmonary arterial hypertension with an odds ratio of 2.28, stronger than total site count. The authors stress the framework is exploratory, not yet a validated prediction tool.
pmc-13472206:
Kanchiralla and colleagues wrote this 2026 correspondence criticizing a life cycle assessment of ship exhaust scrubbers by Stathatou and co-authors. The original study used a well-to-wake analysis. It compared burning heavy fuel oil with a scrubber, a device that washes exhaust, against low-sulfur fuels. It concluded the scrubber option could match one clean fuel and beat another. These authors argue the conclusion downplays risks to the marine environment.

They point out that the original figures showed shipboard impacts for marine ecotoxicity and nutrient enrichment several times higher with scrubbers, yet those categories were set aside as too uncertain. The letter also challenges a dilution assumption used to lower those impacts, asking why dilution should apply there but not to carbon emissions. They warn the framing could sway ongoing International Maritime Organization debate about scrubbers.
pmc-13473406:
Bonilla and colleagues present a 2026 commentary arguing that Guatemala should tap its scientific diaspora, its trained citizens living abroad, to fix weak public governance. These expatriate professionals stay linked to Guatemala but work in richer systems abroad. At home, the authors describe an administration thinned by corruption, vested interests, and dysfunctional hiring that cannot attract scarce expertise.

The commentary calls the diaspora an undervalued, publicly unrecognized asset: brain linkage rather than brain drain. Structured ways to lend diaspora expertise, short missions, remote advising, and joint projects, could strengthen institutions without requiring permanent return. The barrier is partly design: government jobs pay poorly and hire opaquely, so even willing experts cannot plug in. Building clean channels for diaspora help is the authors' central plea for Guatemala's development.
pmc-13473506:
Villavicencio-Valero and Mondavi-Sobby simulated the early history of Saturn's moon Enceladus, asking how ammonia frozen into its south polar ice shell changes the moon's internal heating. Ammonia, detected in the moon's plumes at no more than 0.5% of their composition, lowers ice's melting point, and the authors tested two solid forms, ammonia monohydrate and dihydrate, across shell thicknesses and ice stiffnesses in 2026 numerical models.

The two hydrates behaved differently. Dihydrate widened the range of conditions allowing convection, the slow churning that redistributes heat, while monohydrate zones reacted more strongly to changes in ice stiffness and shell thickness. Both promoted pockets where melting temperatures could be reached without a globally molten shell. The authors argue that small chemical patches of this kind could explain Enceladus's lopsided activity.
pmc-13474606:
Minghui Yu and co-authors test lung washing as an add-on care in 2026 for hard-to-control allergic asthma. The wash, done through a scope, clears mucus and debris from airways. Patients treated from 2021 to 2024 got either standard inhaler-based care or the wash on top. Symptom scores, lung tests, and side effects were compared between groups.

The wash group gained more on symptom scores and on small airway measures. Gains were largest in patients whose lung scores started worst. A breath marker of airway inflammation did not differ between groups, and side effects stayed similar. Fluid from the wash also revealed which germs were present, guiding later care.
pmc-13477306:
Francesco Cribari and colleagues report in 2026 on heart muscle biopsies in cancer patients with suspected heart inflammation from immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs. The patients came from a prospective fast-track cohort for people with possible heart problems during this cancer treatment. Biopsy was used when the diagnosis stayed uncertain or when results would change cancer care decisions.

Forty-eight of 175 patients had a biopsy, with tissue samples read without knowledge of their clinical details. The team compared biopsy findings with symptoms, blood tests, heart tracings, and magnetic resonance scans. Most patients were women, and breast cancer was the most common cancer in the group. The study maps how definite inflammation on biopsy lines up with scan and clinical features, which may help doctors judge when biopsy adds real value.
pmc-13477406:
Hidetaka Suzuki and coauthors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of quick stroke scales that ambulance crews use to spot large vessel blockages. These blockages need clot-removal treatment at specialized centers, so early field detection shapes where a patient is taken. The team searched English and Japanese literature from 2016 to 2024.

Forty-three studies qualified, and eight tools had enough data for pooled accuracy estimates. The Rapid Arterial Occlusion Evaluation scale caught about three quarters of blockages while correctly clearing about three quarters of other patients. A second scale, Field Assessment Stroke Triage for Emergency Destination, performed slightly lower on both counts. The authors also weighed how the tools would perform at different blockage rates, helping services judge the trade-off between missed cases and false alarms.
pmc-13478406:
Jepma and colleagues published a 2026 study on nursing assistants and end-of-life care planning. Advance care planning records what care a person wants near life's end. Certified nursing assistants know clients' daily wishes well, yet planning often skips them. The team interviewed fifteen assistants in Dutch home care and nursing homes.

Most assistants were not routinely part of planning talks with clients. Many wanted more knowledge and skill to join those talks well. Team culture could either open the door or close it to them. Close bonds with clients and families helped assistants speak up in planning. Time pressure worked against their taking part, the assistants reported. Training offers one clear fix for the knowledge gap found.
pmc-13478606:
Mivalt and colleagues created a pig model of hippocampal epilepsy in 2026, sized so that human brain implants can be tested in a freely moving large animal. Seven pigs received MRI-guided electrodes in both hippocampi and a thalamic target, then six were infused with kainic acid, a seizure-triggering chemical, and one with saline as a control. A fully implantable stimulator-recorder, built for humans, logged brain signals continuously alongside video.

Every kainic acid pig, six of six, entered prolonged seizure activity right after infusion, confirming the induction worked in all treated animals. Four pigs survived to long-term monitoring, and three of them developed spontaneous seizures, totaling 2,733 recorded seizures averaging 27.2 seconds each in the chronic phase. Tissue checks showed patchy neuron loss in the hippocampus, and epilepsy's global burden of 50 to 60 million people frames why such a testbed matters for new devices.
pmc-13479406:
Serhat Şen and Feyza Gülgel Şen published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of platelet-rich plasma used during cesarean delivery. Wound problems follow up to 15 percent of cesareans worldwide. The plasma concentrate, made from the patient's own blood, carries growth factors that aid repair in other surgeries, yet cesarean trials had never been pooled.

Five databases were searched through March 2026 for randomized trials comparing plasma treatment with standard care. Outcomes covered scar quality on three rating scales, early wound inflammation scores, and the integrity of the uterine scar, including niche formation and remaining muscle thickness. Pain scores served as a secondary outcome. The synthesis gives obstetric teams a first quantitative read on whether this add-on step earns its place in the operating room.
pmc-13479706:
Rayan Saleh Moussa and a large team of coauthors published a 2026 qualitative study of why Arabic-speaking cancer patients in Australia rarely join clinical trials. Arabic is the country's third most spoken language, and trial underrepresentation deepens outcome inequities. Rather than asking patients alone, the team interviewed healthcare professionals about the barriers and enablers they observe.

The study deliberately looks upstream, at social determinants such as language services, transport, work, and family structures, instead of blaming individual hesitancy. Professionals described how these forces shape every step from referral to consent. Their accounts identify service-level fixes, including interpreter integration and culturally matched staff. The authors frame trial diversity as a system design problem with named owners, not a community deficit.
pmc-13480106:
Fernando Fernández-Aranda and co-authors introduce a 2026 report on a new live-in unit in Catalonia for adults with long-standing eating disorders. The unit opened in January 2024 inside the public health system. Eighteen patients with anorexia or a related diagnosis stayed three to four months on average and completed clinical interviews plus surveys on health, mood, quality of life, and satisfaction.

Patients had been ill for more than twelve years on average and had tried at least three prior treatments without lasting gain. Almost all were out of work despite varied schooling, and other mental health conditions were common. After treatment, quality of life and body mass index both improved by clear margins. Satisfaction averaged above eighty-five out of one hundred, with warm written feedback to match. Early results hint that dedicated long-stay care can help a group that standard services often miss.
pmc-13481106:
Lisandro Torre and co-authors report a 2026 trial of webinar training for vaccine advisory panels weighing a six-in-one child vaccine. National panels must judge proof across many angles before advising health ministries, and demand for coaching has surged as panels multiply. A five-part online series ran from January to June 2025 for panels weighing a switch from five-in-one plus polio shots to a combined six-in-one.

Panels from thirty-two countries joined at least one session, and nine joined three or more, mostly from the African region with support from the Gavi alliance. Surveys and interviews rated the sessions as useful, with peer stories from other countries prized most. Panels asked for more hands-on guidance on cost and feasibility angles plus pairing schemes between countries. Flexible online cohorts may scale expert coaching faster than site visits.
pmc-13482306:
Rathod and co-authors study a smart rubber in 2026 whose stiffness answers to both magnets and heat, a silicone filled with irregular flakes of electrolytic iron at 40 percent by weight. Unlike the round particles in standard magnetic elastomers, the flakes touch and grip more, which should sharpen the response to a magnetic field. The team swept temperature, strain, shaking frequency, and field strength across wide ranges to map the behavior.

Warming from 30 to 70 degrees Celsius softened plain silicone, dropping its storage stiffness 12.5 percent while its energy-absorbing loss measure climbed 67 percent over the same range. The filled rubber lost stiffness faster, down 18.9 percent, because heat loosened the grip that made the flakes reinforcing at cooler temperatures in the tests. The team also built a time-temperature master curve for the material and notes damping shifts with field strength too, pointing to vibration pads that can be tuned by temperature.
pmc-13483406:
Chen and team tracked which viruses sicken Shanghai children, comparing those treated in clinics with those admitted to hospital. Their 2026 surveillance study enrolled 3,533 children under 15 in Pudong over two years, testing swabs for nine respiratory viruses. The aim was to see whether hospital and clinic cases are really the same illness stream or two different ones.

Viruses were found far more often in outpatients, at about 34 percent, than in inpatients, at about 20 percent of those tested. Flu and the COVID virus dominated clinic cases, while RSV, a virus dangerous to infants, leaned toward hospital cases. Infants filled hospital beds, while teenagers filled clinic visits. Even RSV subtypes split by setting, with different variants leading in each group. Chen argues prevention plans should be tailored separately for clinics and wards.
pmc-13483606:
Yahao Li and co-authors pool published results on deep learning for diagnosing slipped lumbar discs from medical images. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searched major databases through March 2026 and kept ten retrospective studies with usable accuracy data. Magnetic resonance imaging is the usual standard, but human readings vary between observers.

Pooled results showed sensitivity and specificity both near 0.94, with a summary curve area close to perfect. Variation between studies was very large, so the authors treat the averages as exploratory rather than settled. Models checked on outside data lost some specificity compared with same-center checks. Differences in what models were asked to output also drove variation. At typical pretest odds, a positive result sharply raised the chance of disease.
pmc-13486806:
Khushi Goda and co-workers gauge how much blood pressure spread comes from genes and daily life acting as a pair. Most past work treats the two as split forces. This 2026 study uses 24,000 people of mixed roots in the UK Biobank. It sets them against 23 daily-life traits. Spread is split three ways for three pressure marks: genes, daily life, and the pair effect.

Pair effects held 7 percent of spread for the lower pressure mark. They held 4 percent for the upper mark and 3 percent for pulse pressure. The 7 percent share ran near twice the rate from a white British-only check run the same way. Still, the gap fell short of firm proof. A genome-wide hunt for pair effects found no hit past the strict bar. Mixed-root groups may show pair effects that flat groups hide.
pmc-13487306:
Hui and team tested whether a data pipeline can sort university sports departments into meaningful governance types instead of grading them on one linear scale. Sports governance juggles money, fairness, efficiency, and sustainability, which rarely peak together. Their 2026 study generated 348 synthetic schools by model run, seeded with four archetypes from resource-focused to balanced, then checked whether clustering methods could recover those types from the numbers alone.

Both clustering approaches recovered the four planted archetypes, confirming the pipeline works under controlled conditions. Nonlinear performance patterns emerged between the types that a single weighted score would flatten away. The authors stress the patterns describe their model run design, not real schools, since no actual institutional data fed the test. Hui offers the design for future use once real governance data can be gathered, positioning configuration over ranking.
pmc-13487606:
Keston Mwiwa Sinkhonde maps where Malawian households with young children fall short on protein and two key amino acids. Published in 2026, the analysis reuses the national 2019 to 2020 household survey covering 5,952 children aged six to fifty-nine months. Food records are converted through composition tables and adult-equivalent scaling, then judged against international thresholds and plotted by district.

Shortfalls in usable lysine topped 40 percent in every Central Region district, with seven of thirteen Southern districts also above that line. Usable protein inadequacy followed the same central-then-southern geography. Total amounts looked better than usable amounts, since plant-heavy diets limit amino acid availability. District-level targeting beats national averages for nutrition programs, and lysine emerges as the quiet bottleneck nutrient.
pmc-13487906:
Zsolt Molnar and fellow specialists offer a 2026 position statement on hemoadsorption for septic shock, a severe form of sepsis where blood pressure falls dangerously. The treatment passes blood through a cartridge that removes cytokines and other signals driving harmful inflammation. The authors review why the idea is appealing, given the mix of excessive and suppressed immune activity in sepsis.

Evidence so far comes mostly from small studies, registries, and mixed patient groups, so firm guidance is still lacking. The statement stresses careful patient choice, timing, and treatment intensity rather than routine use for everyone. Readers get a clear map of what is known, what remains uncertain, and where larger trials are needed.
pmc-13488206:
Gabriela Reka and colleagues review chromosome microarray results in children with autism at a hospital in Lublin, Poland, in a 2026 retrospective study. The test finds tiny missing or extra DNA segments that standard chromosome views miss. Records covered 234 children diagnosed between 2012 and 2024, and the team grouped results by type, likely importance for development, and the genes involved.

About fifty-nine percent of children had a normal result on this test. Single extra segments and single deletions were the most common abnormal patterns, and several DNA changes together appeared in about thirteen percent. Clearly disease-causing findings explained roughly nine percent of cases. Certain regions recurred, including one tied to brain signaling genes. Clustering split the uncertain findings into distinct subgroups for follow-up.
pmc-13489206:
Zhu and a team in China traced in 2026 a chain that turns eye lining cells rogue and lays scar mats under the retina. The scar state is a grave snag of wet age linked macular disease, where sight fades fast. A fat signal dock, LPA1, sat high in scarred mouse eyes made by laser burns. The team raised or cut each link of the chain in cells and mice to test its pull.

More LPA1 drove the lining cells to shed their sheet form and crawl, the first steps of scar work. The dock acts through two aides: it lifts USP1, a tag stripper, which then shields ZEB1, a form switch, from the cell's shred bin. Cut either aide, and the rogue turn stalled. A drug that blocks LPA1, BMS-986278, curbed scar growth in mice more than it curbed leaky vessel growth.
pmc-13490506:
Maoudj and colleagues presented SPINDER, an open-source six-legged robot with eighteen movable joints built for reproducible insect-like locomotion research. Legged robot studies are hard to replicate when every lab builds its own machine. Their 2026 platform prints its body from plastic and drives legs with hobby servos. It senses the world with a depth camera, an inertial unit, and foot contact switches, while a pattern-generator controller coordinates the legs like a nervous system.

Hardware trials demonstrated stable tripod, ripple, and wave gaits, plus walking in any direction on command. The robot switched gaits smoothly, settling within about two gait cycles of each transition. It crossed structured uneven ground with height changes up to eighteen millimeters, completing every run with body pitch staying under five degrees. All designs and code are published for other labs.
pmc-13491806:
Yahao Li and five colleagues test in 2026 whether ordinary smartphone videos from clinic visits can reveal walking patterns tied to specific gene defects. The condition is osteogenesis imperfecta, a brittle bone disorder of childhood. Pose estimation software extracted step and posture measures from outpatient footage of children with IFITM5 or WNT1 gene changes, with a COL1 group kept as a comparison.

Step width and trunk lean measurements stayed consistent when the videos were artificially degraded, a check on reliability. Children with WNT1 changes walked with a wider stance and leaned their trunks further than the other groups, and the gaps survived adjustment for age, sex, medicines, and surgery. Their surgery-free survival also ended earlier. A trial classifier separated the genotypes fairly well, and the authors propose video gait checks as a low-burden monitoring tool.
pmc-13493806:
Chen and colleagues aim to speed up aircraft design by teaching a neural network to predict airflow over folding-wing aircraft. These planes change wing shape in flight to suit different missions. The usual tool, computational fluid dynamics, simulates air in fine detail but takes heavy computing time. The 2026 team generated training data with fluid simulations using moving meshes, then trained an improved PointNet++ model, a network that reads three-dimensional point clouds, to map wing shape onto surface pressure.

Once trained, the network produced pressure maps in seconds rather than the long runs full simulations need. Its predicted lift coefficient, the number describing how much upward force the wing generates, stayed within a small margin of the simulation results across test cases. The authors present the approach as a rapid screening tool that lets engineers test many wing shapes and reserve expensive simulations for the most promising designs.
pmc-13495306:
Yi Zhang and colleagues chart, in a 2026 study, multifocal germ cell tumors inside the skull, a rare form that strikes in two or more brain spots at once. Proof on this variant was thin, so the team reviewed 48 patients treated at one center across two decades. They logged symptoms, scans, tissue type, treatment, and survival.

Patients were mostly boys and young men, with a median age of thirteen. Excess thirst and urine from hormone failure was the top symptom, then weakness on one side. Two thirds had the germinoma tissue type, and over half got combined chemotherapy and radiation. Ten-year survival ran high, though freedom from return was lower, and worse than for single tumors. Germinoma type and combined treatment went with better outcomes, while immune cells inside the tumor marked worse ones. The authors back tissue-led, combined treatment for this rare disease.
pmc-13495506:
Temitayo Moyosore Adebisi and colleagues test, in a 2026 study in southwest Nigeria, whether a single teaching session can lift body and sexual functioning in women treated for cervical cancer. Care for survivors' daily quality of life lags behind prevention campaigns. Twenty women at a federal hospital's cancer unit took a researcher-built psychoeducation module, with functioning scored before and four weeks after.

Most women were in their late forties to mid fifties, none had had the HPV vaccine, and all were on chemotherapy. Scores nudged in the right direction across body, mind, and sexual domains, though none of those shifts cleared the proof bar. Overall quality of life did improve clearly. Pain and partner support stood out as the strongest social predictors of quality of life. The authors judge the session helpful and worth refining, while the single-group design and small numbers cap what can be claimed.
pmc-13495906:
Atul Verma, Esakkinaveen Dhanaraman, and Yen-Pei Fu build, in a 2026 materials study, a catalyst that splits water into hydrogen when shaken by sound waves. The method, called piezocatalysis, turns shaking motion into separated charges that drive chemistry, offering hydrogen without light or wires. Their catalyst grows from a bismuth framework into a bismuth-rich oxide, then couples with a flaky material called MXene.

The best blend produced hydrogen about thirty-six times faster than the starting framework and several times faster than either partner alone. Tracer tests revealed an unusual route through hydroxyl radicals rather than the standard electron path. The catalyst kept working in tap water and showed promise in seawater. Tests under shaking showed the motion turned into current with little loss. The authors present the blend as a step toward harvesting stray motion as fuel.
pmc-13498906:
Muñoz-Tafalla and colleagues mined the genomes of over eighteen thousand extremophile microorganisms for enzymes that digest PET plastic, in a 2026 study. Extremophiles are organisms living in extreme heat, salt, or acidity. Known PET-digesting enzymes belong to one enzyme family, while a different family, the true lipases, had been overlooked. The team combined genome scans with structural modeling, enzyme-substrate simulation, and validation.

Muñoz-Tafalla found two lipases, named LipBv and LipSh1, that hydrolyze PET, and related enzymes in their clusters shared the ability, supporting entire lipase lineages specialized for PET. Structural analysis pointed to differences in loop shape and active-site openness behind their activity and product patterns. These lipases clustered apart from more than thirteen hundred PETases found in the same genomes and from all known PET-digesters. That widens the search space for enzymes suited to mild, sustainable plastic recycling.
pmc-13500506:
Ganpat Singh Chauhan and co-authors build in 2026 a detector for fake online product reviews that reads sentiment toward specific product aspects rather than whole texts. Shoppers and manufacturers lean heavily on reviews, which invites fabricated praise or attacks. Their model embeds aspect-based sentiment into a graph neural network that maps how words, aspects, and feelings connect inside a review, exposing pairings that feel unnatural in invented text. The network also encodes links among users, reviews, and products.

Evaluated on 21,034 Amazon reviews spanning 30 product categories, the system reached accuracy in the low ninety percent range in the reported averages. It beat the strongest rival baseline on precision and recall by clear margins. Splits were stratified by product and reviewer to prevent leakage between training and test data, and the authors pitch the tool for real-time moderation duties.
pmc-13500606:
Seda Camalan and co-authors test in 2026 whether synthetic eardrum images generated by an artificial intelligence image maker can train better diagnostic classifiers. Examining the eardrum with an otoscope is central to spotting infections and perforations, yet labelled image sets are small and grading is subjective. The team created artificial and composite images with a StyleGAN3 generator and trained a deep image network. Comparisons ran against classic augmentation tricks such as flipping and rotating, and against no augmentation at all.

Synthetic augmentation lifted mean test accuracy into the mid-ninety percent range with a matching F1 score in the reported runs, ahead of classic augmentation and well ahead of the unaugmented baseline. The authors caution that their setup represents an optimistic upper bound, since generated images may leak information about the test distribution. The gap suggests machine-made training images can relieve the chronic data scarcity in ear imaging.
pmc-13501806:
Abdalla R Sulaiman and Ghassan E Bassit report a 2026 dental case involving implant treatment for a patient with primary hyperoxaluria type 1. The rare inherited disorder floods the body with oxalate. Crystals deposit in bone and damage the kidneys. This patient had received a combined liver and kidney transplant plus long-term immune suppression. pmc-13503406:

pmc-13504206:

pmc-13505106:

pmc-13506106:

pmc-13507006:

pmc-13507106:
Nandita Menon, Tatiana D Mayorova, Adriano Senatore, and Anil Kishen model, in 2026 lab work, two-way nerve and immune talk relevant to apical periodontitis, a painful infection at a tooth root tip. pmc-13507206:

Case checks support field use across tube and instrument setups.
pmc-13507306:

pmc-13507806:
Marcello Polenghi and six co-authors publish a dataset of images and power records for solar cells that were damaged on purpose, in 2026 work. The set covers few cells from one solar design, so it suits matched comparison more than broad statistics. It gives image researchers paired views of the same damage, plus plain-language labels to train and test their tools.
pmc-13508006:
Chetan Patel, Ghanashyam Patel, and Nile Desai run a blinded trial of a natural oil-pulling rinse for mouth health, in work published in 2026. pmc-13508206:

Faithfulness to the program and basic adoption were also scored. Surveys, interviews, and cost data added context. The study design shows how health systems can test rollout help itself, not just the program being rolled out.
pmc-13508806:

It beat a deep learning baseline, which scored about 95 percent, and it trained much faster. The authors argue that careful feature design plus classical methods can suit clinics better when training data are limited.
pmc-13509006:
Leite and colleagues combined three computational approaches to sort drug candidates that switch the Abl kinase enzyme on or off through a side pocket. That distinction matters for leukemia and breast cancer drug design. Compounds binding the pocket called the myristoyl pocket either bend a regulatory helix to inhibit the enzyme or leave it straighter to activate it. Co-folding predicted the helix bending correctly and separated true modulators from decoys far better than docking, with discrimination scores approaching perfect for inhibitors. pmc-13514906:

Vecchio's team presents the close-monitoring schedule as a way to gain control well inside the usual year.
pmc-13515106:
Michele D'Alonzo and seven co-authors weigh surgical timing in acute aortic valve endocarditis, in a 2026 multicentre retrospective study. pmc-13516006:

Age bands are defined with care, from neonates in their first month through infants, children, and adolescents. Neonates still cared for in newborn units follow the newborn pathway instead. The guideline presents itself as evidence-based and patient-centred, tuned to Singapore's system.
pmc-13518506:

pmc-13518806:
Mohammadreza Mokhtari, Farkhondeh Amin Shokravi, Hasan Shahbazi, and Azam Saffar build and test a 2026 questionnaire on eco-driving beliefs among Tehran line taxi drivers.
