Starting from 96 draft items, validation steps with 401 drivers sampled across strata produced a final 57-item tool covering eight domains, from knowledge to self-confidence. Factor analysis supported the eight-part structure, and most scales proved reliable. Self-efficacy, knowledge, perceived benefits, and perceived risk predicted eco-driving behavior. Planners can use the tool to design cleaner-driving campaigns.
pmc-13518906:
Ravibala A. Patil and four colleagues simulate in 2026 how fluid flows past six square cylinders arranged in a line, all wobbling sideways together. Such arrays appear in heat exchangers, bridge piers, and offshore risers, where vibration and wake patterns decide safety and performance. The team used the lattice Boltzmann method at a modest flow speed.

Varying the wobble rate against the natural vortex shedding rate produced three regimes: clean lock-on, quasi-periodic lock-on, and non-lock-on behavior. The lock-on range was wider than for a single cylinder. One coherent wake wrapped the whole array, and higher wobble rates merged vortices downstream. The front cylinder felt the highest average drag, with values dipping then rising along the row.
pmc-13519006:
Xinchan Liu and four colleagues test in 2026 whether gum disease worsens fatty liver disease in mice fed a rich diet. pmc-13520306:
Büşra Korkmaz and Ayse Aydın survey in 2026 how health literacy relates to confidence about breastfeeding among pregnant women in Türkiye. Health literacy means finding and using health information well, while self-efficacy means believing one can breastfeed successfully.

Higher literacy scores went together with higher confidence scores across all subscales. The authors propose adding literacy-focused teaching to routine antenatal visits, so parents can judge feeding advice with more confidence.
pmc-13520406:
Arkaitz Cano and colleagues engineer in 2026 a new way to pair two unlike antibody halves. The method helps make bispecific antibodies. Such drugs can bind two targets at once. Wrong pairing pollutes the batch and slows clean-up.

The design moves a short strand from one heavy chain to the other. Added point changes then favour the right pairing. Purity neared 99 percent after a single clean-up step. That step matches standard antibody plants. Key immune jobs and blood life matched natural antibodies. Heat stability dipped a bit, yet the drugs stayed strong under stress tests. Trials on several pairs suggest wide plant use.
pmc-13522506:
Wen Luo and co-authors search for a genetic marker that predicts response to a depression drug in a 2026 study. The authors present the marker as an example of precision medicine, where testing guides who should receive a particular drug.
pmc-13522606:

pmc-13523206:

The authors present the combined approach as a data-driven model for managing harvest labor with human and environmental factors in view.
pmc-13523306:

The author stresses that the results are exploratory and that the tiny real-data sample prevents any firm performance judgment.
pmc-13523406:

pmc-13524606:

pmc-13524806:

pmc-13525706:

pmc-13527906:

pmc-13528006:

pmc-13529906:

Response was checked by bone marrow testing after the first cycle, once blood counts recovered. Readers gain a careful comparison to weigh deeper responses against added toxicity.
pmc-13530706:

pmc-13531806:

The TP63 signal looked stronger in people who had smoked, though the interaction itself stayed unproven. Larger groups must confirm the findings.
pmc-13531906:

The gel eased gum disease bone loss in living animals, preserving bone-building capacity while trimming bone-eating coverage.
pmc-13532006:
Guanghui Shen and co-authors study in 2026 how mismatched distress between parents and teenagers relates to self-injury without suicidal intent. Teen distress alone tracked more self-injury across depression, anxiety, and stress measures. Mismatch itself predicted higher self-injury for all three dimensions, whichever side felt worse. For anxiety the harm curved upward at extremes in either direction. Family work on shared emotional understanding is the authors prescription.
pmc-13536706:

pmc-13537106:

The authors propose platelet activation gluing to killer cells contributes to their dysfunction.
pmc-13537906:

Its cells favored a surface pattern linked to stronger killing, showed far higher sensitivity to tiny viral signals, and killed more strongly inside lungs. Polymerase cells favored a different surface pattern with weaker performance. The authors argue that target choice should prize cell quality over cell count alone.
pmc-13538706:
Wenlai Cui and colleagues compare warm-up priming plans for tennis serve play in a 2026 test. Serve speed and accuracy were tracked across every setup and time point.

Serve speed rose after priming in all setups. Ballistic work beat heavy work overall, with its edge focused in the first nine minutes and strongest for upper limb and full body routines. Accuracy shifted over time but never differed clearly between setups at matching times. The authors advise ballistic upper or full body priming shortly before serving.
pmc-13539806:

After the procedure he became confused and lost memory, signs pointing to damage in the thalamus on both sides. Scans confirmed that pattern, caused by blockage of a variant vessel called the artery of Percheron, which feeds that region in some people. He recovered well with supportive care and rehabilitation. The authors warn intervention teams to watch for this rare clot complication.
pmc-13539906:
Ender Eren Ozcelik and seven colleagues map, in a 2026 bibliometric study, how research on immune treatment for solid tumors grew over twenty-five years. Their source was a title-based search of the Web of Science collection, checked against a high-impact subset from Scopus.

Topic maps shift from an early cytokine period to checkpoint drugs, then toward the tumor surroundings and treatment given before surgery.
pmc-13540206:
Fatemeh Navab and six colleagues examine, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how swapping one protein food for another relates to the acid load of the diet in people on haemodialysis. Failing kidneys handle acid poorly, and protein choice is one lever patients can adjust.

Statistical swaps that kept calories equal produced counterintuitive results: replacing red or processed meat with dairy, legume, or nut protein tracked with higher odds of a heavy acid load. Directions reversed for several meat-for-plant swaps. Albumin levels strongly modified these patterns, the authors report.
pmc-13540406:

Long-term exposure hurt more than brief spikes. Nitrogen dioxide tracked with the same three outcomes under long exposure, while coarse particles looked weaker and ozone evidence was mixed. Heavy differences between studies temper the numbers. The authors back tighter standards aligned with world health guidance.

Adding the index to a basic model improved some accuracy measures but not others, a mixed result the authors report plainly alongside robustness checks.

pmc-13555906:

The authors judge integration workable and frame it as the route toward universal coverage.
pmc-13556006:

pmc-13569106:

pmc-13572206:

Staff of the United States Food and Drug Administration issue draft guidance on patient-reported outcome measures. Such measures capture how patients feel and function, as reported by patients themselves. Drug makers may use them as endpoints in trials to support claims on product labels.

The guidance explains how the agency judges these tools and what it currently expects from sponsors. It covers how a measure should be built and how trial results may back a label claim. Clear rules help firms design trials that truly reflect patient experience, not only lab values.
pmc-2270306:
Mossong, Hens, Jit, and co-authors measure social contacts that matter for spreading infectious disease. Models of diseases passed by breath or close contact, such as pandemic flu, guide choices about vaccines and closures. Contact patterns are known to drive what those models predict.

The team gathered real data on who meets whom, by age and setting, across everyday life. Such data replace guesses in models with observed mixing. Better contact data lead to better forecasts of how fast an outbreak grows, which groups drive spread, and which interventions help most.
pmc-3111406:
Boulkedid, Abdoul, Loustau, and co-authors review how the Delphi method is used and reported for choosing healthcare quality indicators. The Delphi technique is a structured process in which experts answer rounds of questions until views converge. It is commonly used to build quality indicators, yet guidance for users was thin.

The authors describe how studies report their Delphi work and discuss its strengths and gaps. Inconsistent reporting makes indicator sets hard to judge or copy. Their review pushes for clearer standards, so measures used to grade hospitals rest on a sound process.
pmc-3995906:
Assarsson and co-authors reported a new protein test in 2014 that can measure many targets at once. Care that is tailored to each patient needs large amounts of high-quality data on markers in blood and tissue. Older tests often measured one protein at a time, which was slow and costly.

Their proximity extension assay measures ninety-six proteins in a single run, all in one format. The method uses pairs of probes that must bind side by side, which keeps the signal specific. Tests showed high sensitivity and good scaling to large sample sets. Such panels can speed the search for marker patterns that warn of disease early.
pmc-4086106:
Robert and Gouet presented a new version of ENDscript in 2014, a web server for studying protein structure. Proteins have levels of structure, from their amino acid chain up to folded units and complexes. Pulling all that information together by hand is slow and error prone.

ENDscript two gathers and draws a full analysis in an automated way, from the basic sequence to the assembled form. The upgrade was rebuilt to improve speed, accuracy, and ease of use. It also adds interactive three-dimensional viewing. Structural biologists use such views to spot the features that govern how a protein works.
pmc-4987906:
Afgan, Baker, van den Beek, and their colleagues updated the Galaxy platform in 2016. High-throughput technologies, above all next-generation DNA sequencing, had brought disruptive change to biomedical research. Reading the huge datasets they produce takes sophisticated statistical and computing tools.

Galaxy offers those tools through a web platform designed to be accessible, reproducible, and collaborative. Users run complex analyses without programming, and every step is recorded so others can repeat it. Sharing workflows helps teams check and build on each other's work. Galaxy brought data-heavy biology within reach of labs without dedicated computing staff.
pmc-5081106:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2016 on worldwide trends in diabetes since 1980. One global target for non-communicable diseases is to halt the rise in adult diabetes prevalence by 2025 at its 2010 level. The team estimated trends and judged how likely countries are to meet that target.

Their pooled analysis covered hundreds of population-based studies with millions of participants. Such scale reveals which regions drive the global rise and where progress stalls. The results show the scale of change needed in diet, activity, and care. Governments use these trend estimates to set and check national diabetes plans.
pmc-517706:
Edgar presented MUSCLE in full in 2004, a program for multiple sequence alignment of proteins. Aligning many protein sequences side by side reveals which parts are conserved and how proteins are related. In an earlier paper, Edgar had shown MUSCLE reaching the highest scores then reported on four accuracy benchmarks.

This paper presents the algorithm in more detail. MUSCLE was designed to cut both the time and the memory that alignment takes, without losing accuracy. Faster alignment matters because sequence collections were already growing quickly. MUSCLE became one of the most used alignment tools in biology, a base step for trees, structure work, and gene family studies.
pmc-5491406:
Roth, Johnson, Abajobir, and many colleagues measured the global burden of cardiovascular diseases in 2017 for the GBD 2015 study. In many world regions, the true burden of these diseases was still murky. The team merged data on new cases, total cases, and deaths into consistent, current estimates.

Cardiovascular diseases cover heart attacks, stroke, heart failure, and other causes, ten of which the team tracked from 1990 to 2015. Their estimates show where death rates fall with treatment and prevention and where they still climb. Consistent methods across countries make the comparisons meaningful. Health ministries use such figures to plan cardiac and stroke services.
pmc-549606:
Pao, Miller, Politi, and their team reported in 2005 on why some lung tumors stop responding to targeted drugs. The drugs gefitinib and erlotinib block EGFR, a growth switch. Tumors that respond at first tend to carry changes in the EGFR gene that make the switch easy to block.

Most such tumors grow back in time as resistance sets in. The team found that tumors which had become resistant often carried a second change in the same part of EGFR. That second change lets the switch dodge the drug. The find explained a chief route of resistance and pushed the design of new EGFR drugs built to beat it.
pmc-5642006:
Stephen Burgess, Dylan Small, and Simon Thompson wrote this methods review in 2015. Their topic is Mendelian randomization, a way to test cause and effect using genes as stand-ins for a risk factor. The review compares the main statistical tools researchers use for that job.

Each method rests on assumptions about the gene variants, and the authors explain when those assumptions can fail. They weigh strengths and limits side by side so readers can pick a tool that fits their data. For anyone using genetic data to judge whether a habit or trait truly causes disease, the guidance here helps avoid false claims.
pmc-5753206:
Daniel Zerbino and a large team at Ensembl published the 2018 update of the Ensembl genome resource. Ensembl has collected and shared genome data since the first draft of the human genome. Its aim is to speed research by giving public data away fast and free.

The update reports new genomes, richer gene annotation, and better tools for comparing species. Users can browse genes, variants, and regulation data in a web browser or pull data in bulk. Most genomics papers rely on Ensembl at some step. The yearly updates keep the resource matched to fast-growing data volumes.
pmc-6227606:
The GBD 2017 Causes of Death Collaborators published this mortality analysis in 2018. Countries need cause-of-death figures they can compare to judge their own progress. The study estimates deaths by age and sex for a long list of causes.

Coverage spans nearly two hundred countries and territories over almost four decades. Heart disease and stroke lead the global totals, while child deaths from infection keep falling. The authors flag places where death records are weak and estimates lean on models. Even with those limits, the release is the standard yardstick for global mortality.
pmc-6441206:
Yang Mou, Jun Wang, Jinchun Wu, and coauthors reviewed ferroptosis in cancer in 2019. Ferroptosis is a recently named form of cell death driven by iron and fat oxidation. It looks and behaves quite unlike the classic apoptosis pathway.

Fast-growing work links ferroptosis to many cancers. Some tumors resist standard drugs yet stay sensitive to ferroptosis triggers. The review gathers the core machinery, from iron handling to lipid repair failure. It also lists the hard problems, such as finding markers in patients. The field hopes this death route can kill cancers that evade other treatments.
pmc-7182206:
Bui Quang Minh, Heiko Schmidt, Olga Chernomor, and coauthors presented IQ-TREE 2 in 2020. IQ-TREE builds evolutionary trees by maximum likelihood and is popular for its speed and ease of use. The first version had gathered many features since its release years earlier.

The second version adds new models, including ones for mixed and partitioned data, and faster search methods. It handles the huge alignments of the genomic era without special hardware. Benchmarks show accuracy on par with or better than rival tools. Phylogenetics courses and labs worldwide treat it as a default choice.
pmc-7719906:

That evidence covered how activity and sitting time relate to health in children, teenagers, adults, and older people.

The document states how much activity each age group should aim for each week, and advises cutting down long stretches of sitting. It also speaks to people living with chronic conditions and disabilities, groups often left out of such advice. National health agencies around the world base their own recommendations on these guidelines, so the numbers chosen here shape public advice for years.
pmc-7764106:
Zeinab Breijyeh and Rafik Karaman wrote a comprehensive review in 2020 on Alzheimer's disease, the main cause of dementia worldwide. The disease slowly breaks down brain cells, and with them a person's thinking, memory, and independence in daily life. It is understood as a condition with many contributing causes rather than a single one.

The review lays out the leading explanations for how the disease begins and advances, including the long debated roles of abnormal protein deposits in the brain. It then surveys the treatments in use and under study, and what each can and cannot do. For readers seeking one clear account of a complex illness, the review gathers causes, symptoms, and therapy in a single place.
pmc-8010506:
Laith Alzubaidi and colleagues wrote a broad review in 2021 of deep learning, the approach that had come to dominate machine learning. Deep learning trains layered networks on large amounts of data, and it had recently produced standout results in fields from image recognition to language. The authors set out to give newcomers and specialists one shared map of the field.

They explain the core concepts, then compare the main network designs built around convolutional networks for images. They also take stock of open problems, survey real applications, and sketch where the field may head next. A review of this scope serves as an entry point for students and as a checkpoint for researchers measuring how fast the ground is shifting.
pmc-8617206:
Xiaojia Hu and co-authors reviewed in 2021 the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, a fast route by which cells pass messages from their surface to their nucleus. The pathway was discovered more than twenty-five years ago and has since proved central to many vital processes, including immunity and blood formation. It works as a rapid module: a signal at the membrane switches on transcription factors that head straight for the genes.

The review traces the pathway from laboratory discovery to the clinic, where drugs blocking its Janus kinase enzymes now treat several diseases. The authors also cover what goes wrong when the pathway is overactive or broken. Few signaling routes have traveled so completely from basic biology to the pharmacy shelf.
pothier-obligations-contracts-1806:
Robert Pothier, a French judge and scholar, wrote his Treatise on Obligations in the 1760s. William Evans's English translation of 1806 is the version here, with notes on English law. Pothier's book is the French civilian foundation of modern contract law.

He defines contracts, consent, error, and fault in clear, ordered chapters. His rules passed almost whole into the French civil code and from there worldwide. English and American judges cited the translation in court for decades. Anyone tracing where modern contract ideas came from will land on Pothier, the quiet professor from Orléans who organized a whole field.
ramusio-navigationi-et-viaggi-vol-3-1606:
Giovanni Battista Ramusio's Delle Navigationi et Viaggi closes with volume three, here in the Venetian printing of 1606. The collection itself dates to 1550 through 1559, when Ramusio issued its volumes in Italian at Venice. He worked from reports sent home by travelers, merchants, and ambassadors of many nations.

Ramusio's three volumes formed the first great voyage collection, the pattern for Hakluyt's and Purchas's later English sets. Marco Polo's travels found their first complete printed home in its pages. Voyages to Africa and Asia fill out the survey. With volume three, the work that taught Europe to read the world as one map stands complete.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: In volume six the valet's memories turn to the later years. Constant recalls the daily habits of a ruler under strain. The private man shows through the public legend. A rare, close look at Napoleon off duty.
rivers-the-todas-1906:
W. H. R. Rivers went to the Nilgiri Hills of southern India to study the Toda people, and his 1906 book reports what he found. The Todas were few in number, pastoral, and organized around the buffalo in a way no outsider had fully recorded.

At the center stands the sacred dairy, where buffalo milk is handled as a ritual by priest-dairymen under strict rules. Rivers also documents polyandry, in which brothers share a wife, and works out Toda kinship with new care. His genealogical method, built for this study, changed fieldwork itself. The book launched British social anthropology's classic period.
santayana-life-reason-vol-5-1906:
Reason in Science, published in 1906, closes The Life of Reason as its fifth and crowning volume. Santayana turns last to science, the pursuit his whole system had to honor without worshiping.

He treats science as reason's most disciplined form: a method for mapping nature's order, powerful exactly because it describes rather than consoles. Against it he sets the claims of history and of the inner life, which science cannot replace. The volume rounds the five books into one vision: reason as man's one guide in every sphere. Santayana was thirty-nine when he finished; few systems begin so complete.
scheible-das-kloster-vol06:
Johann Scheible closed the year 1846 with band six of Das Kloster, cells twenty-one through twenty-four. Halfway through the set, the shape of his work stood clear. He meant to save the whole range of German folk print, high claims and low alike, in full reprints.

The grimoire shelf stays heavy here: spell books, Faust books, and Höllenzwänge in their full, stark text. Beside them sit folk charms and popular chapbooks, the small books that passed from hand to hand. A modern reader meets magic here as it was sold, not as later ages cleaned it. That plain honesty gives the band its lasting use.
schlussel-zu-dem-cabinet-der-geheimen-sc: A 1706 German key unlocked nature's secret treasure chamber. The cabinet of hidden riches. The natural secrets. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care for all readers. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
shahnama-warner-vol-2-1906:
Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner published Volume 2 of their Shahnama of Firdausi in 1906. The Shahnama, or Book of Kings, is the Persian national epic, written by Firdausi around the year 1000. The Warner brothers set out to give English readers the whole poem, in nine volumes.

Volume 2 carries the epic's early kings and heroes onward, through wars, hunts, and court tales told in verse. Their translation kept the poem's shape while making its stories plain to English readers. No full English Shahnama existed before theirs. The volume continues a vast record of Persian myth and memory, where legend and early history flow together without a clear break.
shahnameh-warner-vol2-1906:
Ferdowsi wrote the Shahnama, the Book of Kings, the great epic poem of Persia. Arthur George Warner and Edmond Warner turned it into English verse. Theirs was the first full English verse version of the whole poem. Book two of their set came out in 1906.

Kings rise and fall in long tales of war, love, and fate. Heroes fight beasts and rival lords while wise men warn of pride. The Warners kept the sweep of the tale in plain, strong verse. For most English readers, this set was the first door into Persia's best loved book.
shaku-sermons-buddhist-abbot-1906:
Soyen Shaku was the Zen abbot who spoke for Buddhism at the Chicago Parliament of Religions in 1893. His Sermons of a Buddhist Abbot, published in 1906, gathers the addresses he gave on his American tour of 1905 and 1906. His student Suzuki translated them into English.

Shaku explains karma, rebirth, and the Buddha's enlightenment in a calm, gracious voice shaped for Western hearers. He presents Buddhism as a way of waking, not a set of dogmas to be believed on command. The sermons mark the moment Zen first addressed America through one of its own masters. His dignity did much to win Buddhism a fair hearing in America.
sherrington-integrative-action-1906:
Charles Sherrington was a British physiologist whose lab work mapped how nerves join muscles into working systems. His 1906 book The Integrative Action of the Nervous System sums up years of trials on reflexes. It is often named the founding text of modern neuroscience.

Sherrington names the synapse, the tiny junction where one nerve cell hands its signal to the next. He shows how reflex arcs combine, compete, and yield so that an animal acts as one whole. Later brain science built directly on his terms, his maps, and his careful method. He coined much of the language that nerve science still speaks.
sinclair-jungle-1906:
Upton Sinclair went undercover in Chicago's stockyards in 1904, living among the packinghouse workers for seven weeks. He published The Jungle in 1906, intending a socialist indictment of wage slavery. Sinclair later joked that he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach instead.

Jurgis Rudkus, a Lithuanian immigrant, arrives strong and hopeful, then is ground down by injury, layoffs, and the loss of his family. Around his story Sinclair documents the meatpacking industry in revolting detail: spoiled meat, filth, and worse sold as food. Congress rushed through the Pure Food and Drug Act and meat inspection within months. The Jungle remains the most consequential protest novel in American history.
spr-proceedings-vol20-1906:
Volume twenty of the Proceedings, from 1906, consists of part fifty three alone. The Society for Psychical Research often filled a whole part with one great report. Telepathy and trance work dominate the society's business in this period. Long sittings with mediums appear in near verbatim form.

Investigators weigh the Piper material and its rivals with care. Spontaneous cases of apparitions arrive in smaller numbers, well documented. The volume's single part format suits readers who want depth over range. It forms one brick in the archive wall built between 1882 and 1930. The society's standards, set early, hold firm here. Evidence first remains the rule.
suess-face-of-earth-vol2-sollas-1906:
Volume 2 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1906. Eduard Suess turned in this volume to the oceans, their history and their floors. The work surveys the Atlantic and other seas as archives of the Earth's past.

Suess traced marine transgressions, the long advances of sea over land recorded in layered rocks. He compared coastlines and fossil seas across continents to rebuild vanished oceans. One of them, the Tethys, became a lasting term of geology from his pages. Sollas's translation kept pace with the German original's ambition. The volume shows geology thinking at planetary scale a generation before plate tectonics gave it a new engine.
the-amateur-cracksman-pg706: The book that introduced A. J. Raffles, cricketer by day and burglar by night, creation of E. W. Hornung. Narrated by his awestruck friend Bunny, these 1899 stories follow Raffles through daring robberies carried out with wit and style. The original gentleman-thief tales, they spawned a whole genre of charming criminals in fiction.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau: The sixth volume finds Rousseau famous, feared, and embattled. His bold writings provoke admiration and fury across Europe. The persecuted philosopher tells his own side of the story at last. A great and lonely mind under cruel siege.
the-pigeon-pie-pg2606: Yonge's tale for the young, set when England was torn by strife. Brave children and loyal hearts carry the story. Wholesome and stirring, in her best Tractarian manner, it taught history with a moral, history with a moral for the young.
the-spirit-of-1906: George Brooks captures the mood of a remarkable year — 1906 — when San Francisco's earthquake, political upheavals, and new inventions made the world feel both fragile and thrilling. His reflections take stock of a nation testing itself. A vivid time capsule of American optimism and anxiety at the dawn of the modern age.
the-wandering-jew-volume-06: Eugène Sue's Wandering Jew, volume six: the plot deepens. The wandering Jew's curse unfolds. Grand melodrama. The serial's middle act, sue's plot deepens, the curse unfolds, grand melodrama, the middle act, Sue's middle act.

Judaism's scripture, the Tanakh, is the same body of books Christians call the Old Testament. Its name joins three parts: Torah, the Teaching; Nevi'im, the Prophets; and Ketuvim, the Writings. Generations of rabbis guarded the Hebrew text letter by letter.

Inside stand creation and flood, the exodus from Egypt, laws for a holy people, songs, proverbs, and fierce prophecy. The arc runs across well over a thousand years of one people's history. No public-domain text is attached to this entry yet, per its evidence. The work itself, law, poetry, and history in one, needs no salesmanship.

A. W. Tozer wrote The Pursuit of God in 1948 as a devotional call to Christians grown comfortable with routine religion. Tozer, a pastor in the Christian and Missionary Alliance, urged readers past mere belief into direct, thirsty pursuit of God himself. The chapters are short and intense.

Each chapter ends with a searching prayer, and the argument asks readers to tear down idols of self: self-love, self-protection, and religious show. Plainspoken rather than academic, the book became one of the twentieth century's most reprinted spiritual works in evangelical circles. Readers meet a mid-century pastor insisting that knowing about God is not the same as knowing God.
tob-10808-50206:
Volume two of von Hügel's The Mystical Element of Religion turns critical and philosophical after volume one's life of Saint Catherine of Genoa. What is mysticism, how does it relate to reason, and how can a church institution house a force that seems to bypass institutions? Von Hügel weighs the claims of mystical experience against philosophy, history, and common life.

The constructive argument balances three elements of religion, institutional, intellectual, and mystical, each correcting the others. Demanding in style and learning, the volume forms the summit of its literature for many readers. Those who worked through Catherine's story in volume one now receive the framework von Hügel built to interpret her.

Volume two of Augustine's City of God, in Marcus Dods's translation, continues the bishop of Hippo's great reply to charges that Christianity caused Rome's fall. Augustine wrote between 413 and 426, after Visigoths had sacked Rome. His answer distinguishes two cities, the earthly and the heavenly, intermingled through history.

Later books trace those cities toward final judgment and eternal peace, arguing that earthly empires rise and fall by providence, not by the old gods' favor. The work effectively invented a Christian philosophy of history. Few books have influenced Western thinking about politics, time, and salvation as deeply, and volume two carries the argument to its end.

Benvenuto Cellini, goldsmith and sculptor to kings, dictated an autobiography in John Symonds's translation that ranks as the most shameless of the Renaissance. Cellini brags, confesses, and settles scores in one breath. Duels, murders, prison escapes, and lawsuits interrupt the workshop scenes, and Cellini casts himself as hero of every episode.

Between the violence stand famous makings: the salt cellar for Francis I and the great bronze Perseus for Florence, whose casting Cellini describes like a battle. Bursting with life and lies in equal measure, the memoir is the age's id talking. Historians discount the boasting and still cannot do without the book.

Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur's 1916 translation of the Prose Edda is the version American students grew up on. Snorri Sturluson wrote the original in thirteenth-century Iceland as a handbook for poets who needed the old myths. Brodeur's copy here rests on a verified 1919 printing.

Gylfi, a king in disguise, questions three enthroned figures about the making of the world, the gods' adventures, and the end at Ragnarok. Later sections unpack the kennings, the compact riddles of skaldic verse. Snorri rescued stories that would otherwise have vanished with pagan Iceland. Brodeur's clear prose keeps the rescue working for each new class of readers.

W. Warde Fowler, an Oxford historian, asked in The Religious Experience of the Roman People what religion actually felt like to ordinary Romans. Household gods at the hearth, festivals marking the farming year, vows in sickness and danger, and the dread of getting a ritual word wrong make up his subject. Rome's faith was practice more than belief.

Delivered as Gifford Lectures, the study is scholarly but humane, resisting both mockery of superstition and romantic overreading. Fowler follows Roman religion from the early republic's calendar to the empire's encounter with Eastern cults and Christianity. Readers get ancient Rome's inner life respectfully reconstructed, a corrective to histories that count only legions, laws, and emperors.

Moses Maimonides, the great Jewish thinker of the twelfth century, wrote his Guide for readers torn between the Torah and Greek philosophy. Many educated Jews felt that faith and reason pulled against each other. In M. Friedlander's English translation, the Guide speaks directly to that conflict.

Maimonides treats hard questions one by one: what words about God can truly mean, whether the world was created, and how prophecy works. He reads Scripture with care and argues that reason, used well, supports faith rather than destroying it. Few medieval books have been debated so long or so fiercely.
tourneur-revengers-tragedy-1606:
Printed in 1607 with no author's name, The Revenger's Tragedy was long credited to Cyril Tourneur. Most scholars now assign it to Thomas Middleton instead. Vindice, the lead figure, has spent nine years grieving for his murdered love, and he returns to court in disguise carrying her skull.

The court he enters is ruled by a lecherous Duke and a brood of grasping sons and stepsons. Plot piles on plot until revenge turns into a bloody masque of killing. Dark wit runs through every scene, and the mix of horror and sharp talk has made the play a lasting landmark of Jacobean drama.
un-ga-res-106:
Armenian deaths under the Ottoman Empire stand at the heart of the text filed here as Resolution 106. The file is not a UN text at all. It is a resolution of the U.S. House of Representatives, H. Res. 106 of the 110th Congress, sent to committee on 30 January 2007. It calls on the President to make sure that U.S. foreign dealings show due grasp of the facts on human rights, ethnic cleansing, and genocide in the U.S. record on the Armenian Genocide.

Adam Schiff led the sponsors of the text, with men of both parties beside him. The short name is given in full: the Affirmation of the United States Record on the Armenian Genocide Resolution. Fights over such texts, and over the word genocide itself, marked U.S. and Turkish ties for years. The catalog's UN label and 1915 year are both wrong.
un-sc-res-106:
Resolution 106 condemns an attack by Israeli regular army forces on Egyptian forces in the Gaza Strip on 28 February 1955. The catalog record dates the entry 1948, but the text itself was adopted on 29 March 1955, by a unanimous vote. An Egypt-Israel armistice panel had found the attack was planned and ordered by Israeli authorities.

The Council calls the attack a breach of the cease-fire terms in Resolution 54 and of the General Armistice Agreement between Egypt and Israel. It calls on Israel to take all steps needed to stop such actions. It also warns that any willful breach of the armistice puts the deal at risk, and that no real peace in Palestine can come unless both sides keep their word.

Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone were banned from world markets on 5 July 2000. The Council voiced concern at the part played by the illegal diamond trade in fueling the war. Such stones were reported to pass through neighboring countries, Liberia among them. The diamond industry and West African states were already working on the trade's openness.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ordered all states to bar the direct or indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone. The ban would run for an initial eighteen months. One door stayed open: stones covered by a certificate of origin scheme run by Sierra Leone's government were exempt. Freetown was told to set that scheme up as a matter of urgency and to tell the sanctions committee. States and bodies were asked to help it do so. The move was an early step toward the global Kimberley controls on conflict diamonds.
un-sc-res-1406: Official record keeping at the United Nations preserves Resolution 1406, a Security Council text the catalog dates to 2002. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1506:
Libya's long isolation ended at the United Nations with Resolution 1506, adopted in September 2003. Sanctions placed on Tripoli after the Lockerbie bombing had been suspended for years. Once Libya accepted responsibility terms and a settlement, the Council lifted the measures for good.

Inside the short text, the members remove the arms and travel bans and close the sanctions committee's work. The vote closed a dispute that had run since the 1980s over the bombing of Pan Am Flight 103. It remains the formal end of one of the UN's longest sanctions cases.
un-sc-res-1606: Security Council Resolution 1606 is preserved here from the UN's official record, in a transcription by English Wikisource. Resolutions like this one typically run a few pages: findings first, then a short list of decisions. The entry's completeness is its feature, giving the whole act rather than a headline version of what was decided.
un-sc-res-1706:
Darfur's suffering drove Resolution 1706, adopted in August 2006. The Council voted to expand the UN mission in Sudan to take over from African Union troops in Darfur. Sudan's government, however, refused to accept the deployment, setting up a long standoff.

The text details a force of more than 17,000 soldiers plus police, tasked with protecting civilians and guarding the Darfur peace deal. Because Khartoum blocked it, the plan was later replaced by a joint UN-African Union mission. The resolution preserves the world's first full answer to Darfur, and the limits of voting without consent.
un-sc-res-1806: Resolution 1806, adopted in 2008, is a Security Council act preserved here through English Wikisource's transcription of the record. The number places it among the Council's 1800s run, the output of its later-2000s sessions. The entry gives the full decision at that place: grounds, orders, and the reporting follow-through that such texts standardly require.
un-sc-res-1906:
By Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009, the Council acted on the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Militias in the east still preyed on civilians. Sexual violence, child soldier use, and summary killings went unpunished. The peacekeeping mission faced hard questions about its future shape and size.

The Council extends the mission, called MONUC, until 31 May 2010, keeping up to 19,815 troops. Guarding civilians ranks first among its duties. Joint protection teams and early warning posts, tested in North Kivu, should spread to the south. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010. It will set out what must be done before any drawdown can start safely.
un-sc-res-206:
A thin calm held in Cyprus in the summer of 1965, and the Secretary-General warned it might not last without the peacekeeping force. His report recommended keeping the force for six more months. Cyprus's government wanted it to stay beyond 26 June 1965. Resolution 206 was adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965.

The Council thanked the Secretary-General and the states that sent troops, police, supplies, and money. Its earlier Cyprus resolutions were reaffirmed. The parties were called on to keep showing restraint and to cooperate fully with the force. The force's stationing was extended for six months, ending on 26 December 1965. The longer term matched the warning in the report. A fresh outbreak of fighting was feared if the force left too soon.
un-sc-res-406:
Botswana's call for help was answered on 25 May 1977. The Council had the report of the mission it sent under resolution 403 (1977). Botswana's foreign minister described continued attacks and provocations by the Rhodesian regime. The Secretary-General had written to all states on 18 April with the mission's findings. Solidarity with Botswana was judged essential to solving the Rhodesia question.

The Council voiced full support for Botswana's government as it guarded the country's sovereignty and independence. It thanked the Secretary-General for sending the mission. The mission's assessment and recommendations were endorsed in full. His April appeal to all states, asking urgent financial and material help for Botswana, won the Council's full backing as well. A special account at Headquarters, opened to receive gifts for Botswana, was welcomed. United Nations bodies were asked to act on the mission's plan, and states holding aid back were pressed to respond.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 106, adopted unanimously on 29 March 1955, condemns an Israeli attack in the Gaza Strip. The Council had heard the report of the Chief of Staff of the United Nations Truce Supervision Organization. It had heard statements by Egypt and Israel. It notes the finding of the Egyptian-Israel Mixed Armistice Commission of 6 March 1955.

The Commission had determined that the attack of 28 February 1955 was a prearranged and planned attack. It was ordered by the Israeli authorities. It was carried out by regular army forces against an Egyptian regular army force in Gaza. The Council condemns it as a violation of the cease-fire set by resolution 54 (1948) and of the General Armistice Agreement. It calls again on Israel to prevent such actions. It warns that deliberate violations threaten the armistice system. Any return to permanent peace in Palestine depends on that system.

Blood diamonds are targeted in Resolution 1306, adopted on 5 July 2000. The Council said it was troubled by the role of the illicit diamond trade in fueling Sierra Leone's war, since rebels sold rough stones, often through Liberia, to buy weapons. It also stressed that the legitimate diamond trade matters greatly to many economies and can aid recovery when it is clean.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council banned the direct and indirect import of rough diamonds from Sierra Leone unless they moved under a certificate-of-origin regime controlled by Sierra Leone's government. The ban ran for an initial eighteen months. The scheme helped invent the global certification system later embodied in the Kimberley Process.

More time to study a report is the whole point here. On 30 April 2002 the Council extended MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, until 31 July 2002. The pause let members weigh the Secretary-General's report of 19 February 2002 on the territory's future, while the Western Sahara question stayed under the Council's review.

Sanctions imposed on Libya over the Lockerbie and UTA flight bombings are lifted on 12 September 2003. The measures dated from the early 1990s. Libya had now written to the Council accepting responsibility for its officials' actions, paying compensation, renouncing terrorism, and promising cooperation with further inquiries.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ended the sanctions with immediate effect. It dissolved the sanctions committee that had overseen them since 1992. It also closed its handling of the whole item, removing it from the list of matters before it. The vote was 13 in favour and none against, with France and the United States abstaining.

A truth and justice process for Burundi's past crimes is opened up on 20 June 2005. Burundi's government had asked in 2002, under the Arusha Agreement, for an international judicial commission of inquiry. A report sent to the Council in March 2005 set out recommendations for handling that request.

Lasting peace, the Council says, requires establishing the truth about genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed in Burundi since independence, and bringing those most responsible to justice. The Secretary-General is asked to open negotiations with Burundi's government. He is also to consult all Burundian parties on how to carry out his recommendations, with a report on those talks due by 30 September 2005.

Expanding the Sudan mission into Darfur is decided on 31 August 2006. The African Union force in Darfur was overstretched, and the Council had resolved in May to move toward a United Nations operation there. Sudan's sovereignty, it is stressed, would be unaffected by the transition, and the Darfur peace agreement is pressed to be carried out.

UNMIS is to be strengthened by up to 17,300 military personnel and a large civilian police component for Darfur. The Secretary-General is asked to arrange rapid deployment of extra resources and to consult jointly with the African Union on the handover. The expanded mission's tasks in Darfur include protecting civilians, watching the ceasefire, and supporting the peace deal, though Sudan's consent remained a live dispute.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for another year on 20 March 2008. The Afghanistan Compact remained the shared framework for security, governance, and development, owned by Afghans themselves. The linked fight against the drug trade, which funded the insurgency and corruption alike, is also noted.

UNAMA's mandate, as defined in earlier resolutions, is renewed, and its coordination role across the country is strengthened. The mission and its head are to lead world civilian efforts, support the government's development strategy, and help deliver aid and protection. All Afghan and international actors are called on to work with the mission, and the government is urged to deepen reform, above all in security and justice.

MONUC is extended for five months while its future shape is studied in Resolution 1906, adopted on 23 December 2009. Militias in eastern Congo had still not disarmed. Targeted attacks, sexual violence, and child recruitment continued. Relations with neighbouring states were improving under regional agreements.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 31 May 2010 at up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. It signals a further twelve months after that. The Secretary-General must deliver a strategic review by 1 April 2010, with benchmarks, reconfiguration options, and the critical tasks to finish before drawdown. MONUC's priorities are fixed in order: protect civilians, run disarmament and demobilization for Congolese and foreign armed groups, and support security sector reform. North Kivu protection tools such as Joint Protection Teams and Early Warning Centres must be extended, especially to South Kivu.

Resolution 206 is a UN Security Council renewal for Cyprus, adopted unanimously on 15 June 1965. The Secretary-General recommended keeping the peacekeeping force for six months this time, longer than the usual three, and the government of Cyprus asked for the deployment to continue past late June.

His report warned that the island's quiet was tenuous and that fighting would very likely resume early if the force withdrew. The Council therefore kept the peacekeepers in place and restated its appreciation to the Secretary-General and the states backing the mission. The doubled extension length shows the Council accepting, by mid-1965, that Cyprus needed a longer commitment rather than emergency stopgaps.

Choosing a Secretary-General is the sole purpose of Resolution 306, adopted unanimously on 21 December 1971. The Council had considered whom to recommend as the United Nations' top official. U Thant of Burma was stepping down after a decade in the job, and governments had settled on an Austrian diplomat and former foreign minister as his successor.

In one sentence, the Council recommends to the General Assembly that Kurt Waldheim be appointed Secretary-General. The Charter splits this choice in two: the Assembly appoints, but only someone the Council has put forward. Waldheim went on to serve two terms through 1981, and his tenure later drew scrutiny over his wartime record, which makes this brief appointment text a document historians still revisit.

Resolution 406 passed with no vote on 25 May 1977. It turns a fact-finding trip into real aid for Botswana. A UN team sent months before had sized up Botswana's needs. Rhodesia's white-led regime kept up raids and taunts across the border. Botswana's foreign chief told the Council of the harm in the hall. The UN chief had called on all states in April to stand with Botswana, a small state in the front line of the Rhodesia fight.

The Council voiced full faith in Botswana's right to guard its land, its borders, and its free rule. It backed the UN team's findings and its plan in full. It backed the call for aid just as fully. The aid aimed at roads, water, and farms, so Botswana could stand firm.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
The tenth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/6406, covers the force in 1965 and 1966. UNEF was nearing a full decade on the Egypt-Israel frontier. Few at its birth in the Suez Crisis had expected so long a stay, and its costs drew steady debate.

The report reviews patrols, incidents, troop strength, and the force's budget. It records a quiet border and a mission in working order. It is the last full report in the run: the force was pulled out in May 1967, and war followed within weeks.
virginia-charter-1606:
King James I granted the First Charter of Virginia in 1606 to a group of London merchants and gentlemen. Their company planned to plant an English colony on the coast of North America. The charter gave them legal cover to sail, settle, and govern under English law.

The text sets the colony's borders, names its ruling councils, and promises settlers the rights of English subjects. It also claims rights to mine gold, silver, and copper, sharing a part with the crown. A year later the company's colonists founded Jamestown. The charter is thus a founding paper of English America.
wieger-textes-philosophiques-1906:
Léon Wieger, a French Jesuit who spent his life in China, gathered these Chinese philosophical texts in 1906 and presented them in French. Wieger ran a mission press in Hebei and became known for exact work on Chinese language and thought. His aim was to let French readers meet China's sages in their own words.

The chosen pieces span schools and ages, from early masters to later teachers of the Way and of Confucius. Short lives and notes help the reader place each text. Wieger's versions were trusted for their care, and the set still serves as a window on how Europe first read Chinese thought in depth.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol06:
In 1859 Volume VI of the Journal of Discourses added another year of preaching to the printed record. Liverpool remained the printing base for a Utah church speaking to a worldwide flock. Brigham Young, his counsellors, and the Twelve Apostles fill the pages, their sermons taken down word for word.

The talks show doctrine being worked out in public, applied to marriages, farms, debts, and doubts. That mix of the sacred and the everyday is the Journal's signature across all twenty-six volumes. Volume VI, read in sequence, lets the movement's teaching be watched as it grows.
zohar-de-pauly-french-vol-1-1906:
The Zohar, the Book of Splendor, is the central work of the Kabbalah, ascribed to the circle of Moses de Leon in thirteenth-century Spain. It reads the Torah as a map of the hidden life of God, in the form of talks among Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his companions. Jean de Pauly turned the whole work into French, and his first tome appeared in 1906. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The opening tomes follow Genesis, verse by verse turned to mystery: the ten sefirot, the letters of creation, and the souls of the patriarchs. De Pauly's French is the only complete public domain rendering of the whole Zohar. His six tomes made the book open to Western readers.
